LONDON, February 19.~-F1ood ter
rors replaced rigors of bitter cold over
large part Of Europe today. 1t was
feared that when the toll Of the intn-
dations, real and prospective, was COM
plete, it would equal or surpass that of
the cold.


The Danube and tributaries swelled
over their banks and forced many from
their homes. Melting snow and ice
caused disastrous floods in Macedonia
and Thrace. Bavarian rivers over
flowed, while rising temperatures in
Northern Italy foreshadowed rapid
swelling Of rivers there.


Temperatures Less Extreme.


Temperatures were less extreme than
they have been. but in many localities
the thermometer had not risen to above
zero, or freezing, centigrade.


Advices from the Danube district,
where ice and snow have been piled
feet thick over the surface of the
river, indicated a worse situation, pos
sibly, there than elsewhere. The DAN
ube and It's tributaries had not only
to carry off the huge load of melting
ice and snow, but faced the hazard OF
ice dams which spread its waters over
wide areas before they could be broken.


Widespread havoc was reported from
Thrace and Macedonia, where the
Struma and other rivers overfiowed
sweeping away bridges and hundreds of
cattle and flooding homes. A number
of peasants were drowned Part OF the
City of Cavalla, site of an American to-
bacco depot, was submerged, while
Heraclia was transformed into a vast
lake with inhabitants being fed by
merchants who piled their trade In
boats. Jugoslavian and Grecian sol
diers co-operated to save lives and prop
eity.


Large Areas Flooded.
In Bavaria large areas were flooded
by overf1owing rivers, the situation add
ing greatly to the suffering from what
was still extreme cold.


Meanwhile it was reported from
Stockholm that the ice barrier along
the southwestern and southeastern
coasts of Sweden was growing steadily,
although once day communication
was being maintained with Denmark
and Germany. Numerous steamers
were still stranded, icebound in the Bal
tic Sound and the Cattegat
A huge snowstorm stopped all train
service in Southern Sweden and In some
sections of Scania inhabitants had to
dig their way out of houses through
second-story windows, so deeply they
were buried Continued intense cold
was predicted.

elise Dudley had stopped the Pirate

CHICAGO, January 5.-What prom
ises to be one of the fastest and dizziest
Big Ten basket ball championship races
il years starts tonight with eight teams
in action on four fronts.


Northwestern's Wildcats. who showed
more class than any other Big Ten
team during the preliminary season,
tangles with Michigan'S up-and-coming
team at Ann Arbor; Illinois invades
Purdue; Ohio State invades Iowa, and
Wisconsin clashes with Minnesota at
Minneapolis.


Only Indiana, co-champion with Pur-
due last year, and Chicago do not start
their championship campaigns tonight:
Indiana will rest, while Chicago will
close its preliminary program by meet
ing the Butler Bulldogs.


To those who have been attempting
to pick winner, the championship race
appears to be toss-up. Every team,
with the possible exception of Chicago,
Ohio State and Minnesota, are regarded
as contenders. Minnesota, which hasn't
won the cage title since 1919, got Off
to a poor start, but came back to win
three straight. Ohio State has been far
from impressive, while Chicago lost
much valuable time and experience be-
cause of the influenza wave. which
closed the Midway School for three
weeks.


While Indiana has had poor pre-
li,ninary season, the Hoosiers were be-
lieved to be very much in the race.
Losing two and winning two games,
they scored less points than their oppo-
nents. but they have habit of coming
back to win titles.


Northwestern. Illinois and Wisconsin
were the only three members of the Big
Ten team TO come through undefeated
in the practice schedule and appear
good.


On the basis of past performances.
however, Purdue, Indiana, Wisconsin,
Northwestern and Iowa appear to have
the best chances of landing on or near
the pinnacle. Michigan also has been
improving rapidly and is feared as much
or more than any other team.


Survey of statistics of the preliminary
season reveals Northwestern hung up
the best record, piling UP 1874 points to
IS for its opponents, Wabash, Pitts
bureh, Notre Dame and Penn State.
Ohio State had the poorest record, los
ing two out of four games and scoring
liz points to its opponents 1913.

officers and tried to escape, but his
boat was caught in q backwash and
upset.

George Boehm and George Bruno,
stripped of their outer clothing, plunged
in and rescued him. The liquor given

Piece Together Sordid Story.


Authorities pieced together the sordid

ard Polster and Pope's story of lying

The Bradley home in the Capital was

Ben house. and stood at the jib-lot
point where Connecticut avenue and

VeritabIe Art Treasure.


The house during the Bradley

from all corners of the earth. Chief
among the art prizes were the beds
made from the affairs OF old Philippine
Catholic churches. richly decorated in
solid gold and precious stones. The
spreads for these beds were rich altar
cloths taken from the same churches
when the church and state in the
Philippines were divorced following the
taking over of the islands by the United
States.


During their residence In the Capital
the Bradleys were friends of the late
Mai. Gen. J. Franklin Bell. who saw ser
vice In the Philippines and aided the
Bradleys in their collection Of the treas
ures of the Philippines.


Theater Built In Home.

ing capacity Of 500. where amateur

days there were musicales with Mary
Garden and members OF the Metropoli-

turned over to the British embassy for
use Of extra clerks during the war and
the rest of the house was closed.


It was about six year ago that Mr.
Bradley started the removal Of the house
from Washington to Newport. Under
his personal direction the project was
completed in about three years, although
the actual razing of the house here
was accomplished in q comparatively
short time.


Mr.. Bradley and . daughter, Mrs

Rev. Herbert Shipman. Suffragan Bis

tinental. north and south on the Pacific
Coast, the same on the Atlantic Coast,

from the Great Lakes to Florida.

In the country is between Boston and
Jacksonville, Fla. via New York, Phila-
delphia, Baltimore, Washington, Rich
n1ond and Atlanta.

face each other and let the best man

NEW YORK, January 28.-Capt.
George Fried and his mates of the
Florida rescue were headed into another
storm today gale Of cheers and a
blizzard of ticker tape.


Their course lay over the famous
heroes trail, from the Battery Up Broad
way to the City Hall, to permit the city's
thousands to voice their admiration for
the skill and daring which saved 80 lives
from the sinking Italian freighter 100
miles of the Virginia capes last We'd
nesday.


The sound of his name echoing amid
cheers against the walls of Broadway
SkyScraperS was not new to Capt. Fried.
Three years ago he met similar re-
ception when he docked the liner Pres
tdent Roosevelt after taking 25 off the
British freighter Antinoe.


Aides Share in Glory.


Sharing in the plaudits of the crowd
and the honorS which the city heaped
upon the captain were Chief Officer
Harry Manning, who commanded the
life boat in it's perilous trip to the side
OF the sinking freighter; Nelson H.
Smith, chief radio operator, and the
eight members of the boats crew.


The program for the parade and re-
ception called for the bringing of Capt.
Fried and his men from Hoboken to
the Battery on the city tug Macon at
noon. An escort composed Of Regulars
from Governors Island and sailors from
the navy yard was ordered for the
march up Broadway.


At city hall Mayor Walker and other
city oft1cials arranged to extend the
greetings Of the city to the heroes and
present them with gold medals Illumi-
mated scrolls extolling their dead also
were prepared for presentation to Capt.
Fried, Manning and Nelson.


A luncheon was arranged at the Ad-
vertiSing Club after the city hall re-
ception.


Three Heroes Speak Over Radio.


After a day spent resting at their
homes, Capt. Fried, Manning and Mel
son spoke over the radio last night
Capt. Fried urged that all credit for
the rescue be given to Manning and
the oarsmen of the lifeboat.


In his talk, Manning described how
the small boat was driven through
the darkness and mounting seas, to the
side Of the sinking ship, how a line
was passed aboard and how the Italian
sailors plunged into the water and were
drawn into the rescue boat.


He paid warn tribute to the pluck
of the shipwrecked men, six of whom
made the dangerous leap despite seri-
GUS injuries.

in an Italian hospital being treated
for injuries and exposure, ~ mem
bers Of the rescue crew attended church
services twice yesterday. In the eve-
ming they were the guests of Broad

GIBRALTAR, July 1.-Spain and this
little colony today eagerly awaited ar
rival tomorrow of H. M. S. Eagle, air
plane carrier, with Maj. Ramon Franco
and his three companions of their
Inflated transatlantic flight attempt
aboard.


The Eagle radioed 1t was making
ordinary progress on its way from a
point 100 miles southeast Of Santa
Maria Island, Azores, where Saturday
morning it picked UP the four aviators
and their Dornier Wahl plane. They
had been down on the water seven days.


Warm Reception Expected.


There were indications a tumultuous
reception would be accorded the airmen
when they arrived here, with the Span
ish premier, Gen. Primo Rivera, and
members Of their families from Madrid
and other cities among those greeting
them. There has been demonstration
after demonstration among the Spanish
residents here since radio advices Sat
urday told of finding the lost airmen,
who had been given up for dead


There was the keenest curiosity to
learn the detailed story of the aviators,
the only word received here being the
official statement given out by the Brit
ish admiralty at London. This mem
toned starting and landing times, but
contained little real information of the
flight, beyond that q strong wind had
caused them to fly over the Azores with
out knowing it. There was general ex-
pectation that the story of the seven
days spent on the Atlantic wastes would,
exceed any other air adventure Of re-
cent months.


Rescuers Are Cheered.


At Madrid yesterday thousands Of
Spaniards from every walk Of life par
ticipated In mammoth demonstration
OF Joy and Thanksgiving at finding the
missing airmen. The manifestation was
organized by the Spanish Aero Club as
a public expression Of Spain's gratitude
to the British, French, Portuguese and
Italian governments for their aid in
the search for the men. Cheer after
cheer was given for the British Navy
and the British air force before the
British embassy, Ambassador Sir John
Grahame responding.


It was said the other two Spanish
Transatlantic aviators, Capts Jiminez
and Iglesias, would come here for the
arrival Of the Eagle. Delegations from
Cadiz, Madrid and 80 or 40 other Span
ish towns were also expected.

federal authorities today denied that
Gov. Abelardo Rodriguez of Baja Cali
fornia had conferred with Jose Gonzalo
Esccbar,. generalissimo of the Inflated

er, reported last, night that EScobar,

across the border last Thursday. The
rancher, who said he met the rebel gen.
eral, declared the conference was ar
ranged by an American mining engi-
neer.


United States customs and immigra-
ton officials at Gila Bend said they did
not believe EScobar has entered this
country. They pointed out that for sew
eral weeks they had watched closely
for airplanes from Mexico and that no
such plane as might have brought Es-
cobar across the border had been sight
ed. The terrain surrounding Gila Bend
Is such that plane landing many miles
from the town could be seen.

is now at ranch between Gila Bend
and Ajo, AriZ., the United States officers
said there were no ranches in the desert
country between the two towns.


Uhrlaub reported that Escobar told
him he would claim the protection of
the United States by "the same right
the Kaiser of Germany claimed that of
Holland at the close of the World War"

riguez refused Escobar permission to
enter Baja California.

NEW YORK, February 20.-As the
National Hockey League season goes
down the home stretch the complaints
about the lack of scoring are due to in
crease The teams, with playof posi-
lions at stake in nearly every contest
are not taking any chances with open
play, and the spectators who favor
numerous goals are the sufferers.
Last nights three games provide a
good sample of the closing battles. Only
I'VE goals were scored by the six teams
involved, and more than half Of these
were tailed in the battle between De-
troit and Ottawa. The Senators, tail
enders of the International group, cut
loose with two counters before Detroit

gin. The Bruins now are only 2 points

scored the only goal on much disputed
play. The Pirates claimed that the
referees whistle had blown before
Shore shot, and a penalty to Hib Milks
of Pittsburgh backed up their claim,
but the goal was allowed. Before the
dispute ended the police were called
upon to protect one Of Bostons noisily
loyal rooterS from a Pittsburgh player
who tried to climb into the stands.

national group. the Montreal Maroons
did a good turn for their townsmen,
Les Canadiens, by downing the New
York Americans by 1-to-0 count. The
result gave the MaroonS tie with
Toronto for third place In the division
and left the Canucks two points ahead
of the Americans. Bill Phillips did the
| scoring in the middle of the first frame
and put the contest on rush and
guard basis for the remaining so min
utes. With the aid of George Boucher,
veteran back line player just acquired
from Ottawa, the MaroonS were able
to equal the Americans at defensive
playing and except for a few bursts of
speed, the defense was the principal

stage.

New York and during her career took
part in at least 70 plays. She was one of
the first American actresses to appear
in IbsenS plays.

Shaw of Boston, survive her.

ARLINGTON COUNTY COURT
HOUSE. Va, February 5.-With the
arrest of four youths, Arlington County
police claim to have solved the recent
robbery of five business houses in the
county. They have recovered loot worth
nearly $1,000, they say.


Those under arrest, all minors, are
Milton Rothery, Waverly Hills, Va;
Alton Parker Riddle, Waycroft, Va,
and Harry Smallwood and Walter Her
riety, both of Ballston, Va. All were
arraigned before Police Judge Harry II.
Thomas in Police Court this morning
and waived preliminary hearings. Roth
cry and Smallwood were held under
$1,000 bond each and Riddle and Her.
riety under $4,000 bond each.


The burglarieS with which the boys
are charged started before Christmas,
the last taking place little more than
a week ago. Rothery, SmallWood and
HEREBY are accused of having entered
and robbed a clothing store in Ballston
and the two former With entering a
hardware store and barber shop in the
same town. Rothery and Riddle are ac-
cused of entering a garage near the
courthouse and Smallwood and Rothery
with breaking into a shoe shop on VIII
son boulevard near Glebe road.


Rothery, Smallwood and Herriety were
arrested by Deputy Sheriff Harry Wood
ward and Policemen c. w. Carr and
Raymond Crack. Riddle was arrested
by Washington police at the request Of
the Arlington County authorities. -. :.

grade.

ships, suddenly released by the Spring
thaw from their ice-bound mooring,

liding with other boats and catapulting

bridges with such force that five OF
them sank.

blocks Of floating ice. passenger
steamer between Belgrade and Zemlin,

great flow, was carried helplessly down
the river and crashed into a concrete
bridge 1t sank within few minutes,
all passengers, however, being saved.

reported spreading rapidly in Northern
and Central Manitoba today. Sparks

country, presenting battling problems

these sections on account of the heavy
clouds of smoke. Rain is needed badly.

Forest, patrols have the fires under
control, and the blaze in the Duck Lake
and Porcupine districts has been headed
off.


At Riding Mountain two new fires
were brought under control quickly,
but there still remains danger of fresh
outbreaks because of the dry timber.


Thirty-three fire fighters narrowly es-
capped death near Rennie yesterday
when flames nearly surrounded them.
They were guided to safety through
heavy smoke by calls of James Barclay,
section foreman, who had been sta
toned as lookout on high rock ridge.

Animal life has been driven into the
open by the flames, and several lumber
camps have been destroyed.

CANTON, China (P).-There will be
little relief for China's starving mil
lions this Fall if the crop statisticians
are correct in their calculations.


This will be especially true in the
South China provinces of Kwangsi and
Kwangtung, where the principal crop,
rice, is below normal. There are 49,
100000 people in the provinces and the
normal rice crop is about 10000 short
tons.


Spring rainfall this year was IS per
cent less than average in Kwangsi and
Kwangtung, so the farmers have passed
through one of the most serious
droughtS in SO years. Large provincial
cities depending on rain for their water
supplies have faced serious shortages
of the precious liquid and even the
British colony of Hongkong endured a
two-month dry spell that drained every
reserve reservoir.


Back in the interior conditions we're
worse. And now the Chinese farmer is
wondering where his Winter provisions
are coming from. Estimates of the first
rice crop place the yield at between 20
and 40 per cent of normal. Coupled
with the fact that there was a 10 per
cent reduction in the yield of the Sec
ond rice crop last Fall, due also to
drought, the shortage this year will
have serious consequences.


Rice farmers near rivers and canals
resorted to irrigation and in their fields
the crop is practically assured. Such
fields, however, are few and far be-
tween and the crop they produce will
be small compared with the amount
needed.

PARIS (P).-Gambling fever has
British holiday makers in its grip and
the gamblers are pouring their shillings
and pounds into France in almost
enough volume to pay the French war
debts to Britain.


Within few hours travel of South
ern England, including London, there
are dozens of French seaside resorts
and all of these resorts have casinos.
LIE Touquet, Deauville, Trouville and
Dinard are the chief ones, but there
are scores of smaller ones studding the
Emerald Coast. lie Touquet Casino
alone made $4,000 900 last year and the
French government collected more than
that in taxes.


British consuls are kept busy send
ing the losers back to England. Bel
GUM has now added to the facilities for
taking the British tripper's money by
making roulette legal in all Belgian
casinos. Roulette has hitherto been
more or less confined to Monte Carlo.


There seems to be not the slightest
chance of reform wave striking France
and causing prohibition of gambling,
which happened periodically before the
war. The reason Is that the govern
ment makes millions from gambling by
taxation, and the government needs the
money badly.

| the tragic death of Edwin Hill, 20

lete at the college.
Hill was on the way to his apart
ment here last night, accompa MED
by John ,Bunyan, former New York
University student. The youths
stopned to chat with Patrolman
Joseph Green, with whom they were
friendly, at a police booth near the
campus.
Girls Pass
During their conversation, two
girls passed.


Hill hailed the girls IN kidding
way, according to Green and Bun.
van, and then facetiously asked
Green for his police club so he
could "disperse them"


Despite Green's protest, Hill seized
the clubs. Green said he sought to
recover the club and that Hill, laugh
ing at his protest, reached around
with his free hand and jerked the
policeman s revolver from its holster.


Green caught the hand with which
Hill grasped the gun but the sturdy
football star held tight to the weapon
and the two srappled.


For q few moments they swayed
back and forth. Then there was a
sudden flash as the gun went off and
the Mortified patrolman saw Hill
crumple to the ground.


Green raced to a telephone and
called an ambulance. DIR. Sanamore
OF Fordham Hospital responded but
the youth was already dead. DR..
Sanamore said Hill had probably
died instantly.


An immediate inquiry into the
shooting was started by Deputy
Police Commissioner Felix Muldoon
and Deputy District Attorney John
McGeehan. Bunyan verified Green's
story that the shooting was acci.
dental.


Hill Was Senior.


Hill, a senior student of commerce
at the university, was the son of
Charles j. Hill, wholesale grocer of
Burgesston.

sity letter in two sports. football
and baseball. and ranked next to
Ken Strong among the college ath-
letes.

NEW YORK, December 14-With the
rails strong the entire session and the
industrials, though irregular at times,
closing strong, todays stock market
gave good account of itself.


Features at the end were buying of
the motors, particularly General Mo-
tors and Chrysler, the recovery in
United States Steel, which had been
heavy earlier in the day, but which left
of with substantial gain, and the rally
In the electrical manufacturing stocks.
Utilities also did better in the last quar-
ter of an hour.

Buying of the rails, which was in
evidence from the start, was presum-
ably based on the expectation that
the Interstate Commerce Commissions
merger plan would be announced
shortly. Judging from the way stocks
acted, this was considered favorable
development, although no one profeSsed
to know the details of the commissions

to points and in the non-dividend
payers Wabash, the st. Paul issues,

Erie up to 4 points. Part of these
gains was lost in the late realizing.


Most of the time the industrialS we're

ly. American & Foreign Power was one

rapidly first above and then below the
preceding close. General Electric and

the start and then sold off.


Short Covering.


United States Steel opened unchanged
but later lost a point or two on com
paratively small volume. Short cover
ing came into Fox Film, stimulated per-
hapS by the suggestion that the ex-
change might renew its inquiry into the
extent of bear operations. The oils did
little. Motors were we'll supported, with

Such news as there was ought to have
helped the market. The weekly trade
| reviews reported a better sentiment,
and attention was paid to a statement
from Washington that Christmas buy-
ing was going on at satisfactory rate.
Traders liked the way the market acted
a1ter the weakness of only two days
ago.

| July 2, 1S63.--Extra editions of the
newspapers today still failed to give
detailed information regarding the great
battle in Pennsylvania near the town
Of Gettysburg between the Union Army
under Gen. Meade and the Confederate
Army under Gen. Lee. There were in
dications, however. that the issue may
| yet be undecided. The latest information
aVallable here uD to late hour this
afternoon was that the Sd and 18th
Corps Of the Union Army were moving
up about 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon
to engage in the fight.


Military authorities here are hopeful
that the next official advices will tell
OF substantial Union victory They
base this hope on the apparent fact
that when the Sd and 18th Corps of the
Union Army were moving up fresh TO
engage the Confederates the Union
troops that had already been engaged
seemed to have successfully held the
ground from which the Confederate
generals, Longstreet and Hill, were at
tempting to drive them

9 o'clock yesterday morning. probably
on the road between Gettysburg and
Chambersburg and nearer the former
place. At that hour Gems. Longstreet
and Hill are reported to have launched
an attack on the 1st and 18th Corps Cf
the Union Army. The engagement at
once became very severe. The Union
loss has been heavy, including Gen.
REYNOLDS killed.


With the greatest eagerness and
anxiety later news of the great battle
is awaited here by Army headquarters
and the public. The impression prevails
generally that the issue on this field
will have greater consequences than
anv battle thus far in the war.

BELFAST, Me. (P).-Two fam
lilies here have been discovered
that having two loud speakers
hooked to one radio set may turn
into a means for overhearing
what is going on in the neigh
boris household.


Under the arrangement carried
out, one family has the set and
one speaker, and other family, by
using an extension line has a
loudSpeaker attached to the same
set. The set was shut off one
recent Sunday afternoon when
the family in whose home the set
is located heard music issuing
from the loudspeaker. The sound
was cornet playing scales.


After puzzling a while the other
family was asked If any one there
might be practicing on a cornet.
The head of the house was doing
just that. Investigation showed
that the two loadspeakers formed
a telephone circuit and that when
members of one family spoke into
their speaker the other family
could hear.

house, but did not buy it there.

fred" the informers and raided Brooks
\ house after Brown brought back the
liquor, found only two empty half
gallon jars.

BOSTON, September This weeks
United Business Report, in summariz-
ing the opinions Of various business
and financial authorities, forecasts that
general business win continue at cur
rent high levels for the remainder OF
the year.


While drought has substantially re-
duced crop prospects in some districts
the recent increase in agricultural
prices assures total farm income at
least equal and probably slightly above
last year.


In the industrial field the steel, au-
tomobile and machine tool industries
stand out conspicuously on account of
their high rate of operation. Further
more, several Of the newer industries
such as radio, electrical refrigeration
and aviation have gained sufficient size
to become important factors in the
business situation.


The two major unfavorable factors
are high money rates and reduced
building activity. In neither of these
cases, however, has the influence on
the general business situation been suf-
ficient to Offset the many favorable
factors.

One Virginia post Office was robbed
and completely destroyed by fire and
another was ransacked and $4,000 taken
in two spectacular thefts shortly after
midnight last night.


The post Office at Aldie, Va, was rob-
bed of $500 and all records and books
burned in blaze that is thought to
have been set by the burglars The
blaze, lighting up the entire vicinity,
burned for nearly an hour before APP
paratus from Leesburg arrived. Fire
fighters fought for nearly three hours
before the fire was conquered. Only
the charred ruins remain.


The building was erected in 1900 and
IS owned by Will Goode of Aide. who
also manages the place. Investigation
by fremen revealed that the safe had
been blown open and its entire contents
taken. This strengthened the theory
that the fire was set by burglars. Others
contend that the blaze originated when
the fuse which the robbers may have
used to blow open the safe, set fire
to books, and receipts lying around the
office. Police are making a search for
the robbers.


The robbery of the other post Office
took place at Luray, about one hour
before the Aldie fire and theft occurred.


The robbers gained entrance through
the front door by jimmying the lock
and blew the safe. Police officials are
of the opinion that the job was ac-
complished by experts. The building is
comparatively new, having ben built in
1926.


A colored woman who lives across the
street from the post Office told police
she saw two men working inside of the
window about o'clock this morning,
but no clue to the identity of the
burglars has yet been found. The loot
consists of 500 in cash and $4,000 in
stamps.

Ostrich feather farmers are among
the most pessimestic people in Africa.
They have been In this undesirable
frame of mind for nearly 90 years,
writes the johannesburg correspondent
of the San Francisco Chronicle; in
fact, ever since the occurrence of the
change in women's fashions that af-
fected this important industry. Paris,
New York and London dress and hat
designers are responsible for this
tragedy to one of South Africa's out
standing activities.


In 1918, the last prosperous year for
the ostrich feather farmers, more than
three quarter million birds we're in
captivity. AS soon as war started in
1914, the luxury merchants of the
world closed their accounts and the
slaughter of the now useless African
birds commenced. Nowadays one often
sees wagonloads of ostrich carcasSes
being transported over the rural high
ways surrounding Oudtshoorn, Cape
Province, the former headquarters OF
the industry.


From 1880 till 1918 ostrich farming
was admittedly the most prosperous
branch of agriculture in all Africa. A
single pedigree bird was worth from
SIS, 900 to $1,000, and the land on which
the creatures thrived sold at $1,000 an
acre. Almost every ostrich farmer
lived in mansion and in view of the
fact that noticeable competition never
arose in any other country the settlers
showed the certainty of continued
wealth. Strict government embargos
prevented the export of live birds or
eggs to states where competition was
possible. Apart from that the Calf
fornian, Australian, Argentine and AL
gerian experimenters were handicapped
by climatic disadvantages


Africa'S prosperous growers did not,
however reckon on one thing. While
| they continued to give out money on
mortgages to buy costly automobiles,
and to send their sons to college,
fashion veered around in favor of small
| hats for women. Nobody bought the
picture models of 1912 any more and
even for trimmings and fans the in
| quiries were few


While the guns in France crashed,
the homesteads in Oudtshoorn district,
South Africa, became silent. Nobody
! wanted frills and furbelows from 1914
to 1918. The breeding paddocks in
| which the birds had once been kept
were now used for tobacco and other
ordinary crops. The great American
and French dealers who formerly main
tanned branches in this country closed
their Offices and the huge Feather


Market Hall at Port Elizabeth, the
! harbor through which all the produce


was once shipped, was devoted to every


day purposes. Since then the farmers


have again tried to popularize the once


remunerative product.

LIVERPOOL, May 21.-After send
ing a wireless warning to all ships in
the vicinity to give her wide berth, the
British steamship Alberto from New
York safely reached the Mersey under
escort today with rudder trouble.


Some time after she had left Cobb
yesterday a large pin connected with
the steering gear slipped and her rud-
der was put out of commission. The
ship was stopped for half an hour while
emergency gear was put into operation.
Meanwhile tender was rushed from
Liverpool to meet the disabled vessel
and piloted her into the Mersey.


After discharging her passengers, the
Alberto docked for examination and re-
pairs.


s(The Alberto, 1924 tons. sailed
from New York on May ii and from
Boston on May II for Cobb and Liver
pool)

Three of 600 West Indian negroes

were near death this morning.
Many others were nursing minor
injuries and Is were under arrest.


Police reserves. armed with rifles
and a sub.machine gun, broke up

buildings participated by throwing
bottles and other missiles from the
windows.

bers of the Universal Negro I'M,
provement Association. strutting In
their blue uniforms with glistening
gold braid and brandishins unloaded
rifles, attempted to force an en-
trance into Liberty Hall. The Gar
vey Club, a rival negro organization,
was holding a meeting in the hall
and it's 500 members were similarly
armed.


The 100 members of the Universal
Association, which recently broke

parent organization, wanted to take
the hall and were overwhelming the
smaller band, belaboring them with
rifle butts and sabers, when the
police riot squad with gas bombs
and machine guns broke up the
party.

swinging their fists and pulling the

German toy makers have discovered
magnetism. In the shops of German
cities there appeared recently a pair
of fiat pasteboard dolls named "Hansel"
and "Gretel," each provided with sew
eral outfits of clothes. Built into the
dolls are small permanent magnets.
Sewed into the margins of the coats
and dresses are thin strips of iron.
Whenever these clothes are put on the
dolls they are held fast by magnetic
force, no pins buttons or other fasten-
ers being necessary Long-suffering hui
man beings striving with difficult COL
lar buttons will probably sigh for SIM
liar devices for themselves.


Another group of the new magnetic
toys consists of family of athletes,
like these who build human pyramids
and go through other antics In cir
cuses. Inside these dolls are small but
powerful magnets made of the new
metals which retain their magnetism
for years. When these dolls, contain
ing invisible magnetic muscles, are
placed on top of one another, Just as
the real athletes place themselves in
their groups, the magnetic forces hold
the dolls in position as though they
were glued together


With little ingenuity the fortunate
youngster who owns a set of these toys
can construct whole series of human
pyramids and "Strong-man' acts for
himself.

Youngsters In the mountain regions no

their vocabu tries have become purged
of naughty words through the work
of club women of Tennessee.

of the Margaret Henry endowment
fund of the Tennessee Federation of
Women's Clubs, reports also that the
calico wrapper, once the sole garb of
the mountain woman, has given way to
hats and dresses which the
women make with their own. hands.


In 1928, when Margaret Henry be-
gan the mountain division work. she
found-no schools, people without ed
. ucation walking miles to have their
letters read deformities among chill
dren in nearly every home, sickness
rampant, food cooked in one pot for
several families over a gypsy fire. Mrs.
Stewards report for 1928 shows an
eight months school term with 100
per cent daily attendance, crude. but
clean homes, mothers and fathers
reading and answering letters, disease
under control, grammar school aver
ages some Of the highest made In the
State.

When your car gets out Of order you

bile. Nature gives you warning-not by
words, but by signals or symptoms Your
doctor recognizes these danger signals and
you should also know them and instantly
heed them. 1t may save you much pain,
serious illness and perhaps big repair bills.


When the bile becomes stagnant in

ant, your tongue coated, bad taste in

bladder making you get up frequently,

morning you are tired instead of re-

faction and self-poisoning or " intestinal
toxaemia, " as the doctors call it. High
blood pressure, with headache and swoon-
ing spells, may result from continued
neglect.

probably following the general outlines

esty and economy, with industrial and
farm development encouraged as q

LITTLE AMERICA, Antarctica, No
vember 29.-The material taken in the
plane onComd r. Byrd's polar flight
consists largely of supplies and equip
ment which might be needed in the
event of a forced landing.


If it were not that this contingency
remote. it is hoped-must be provided
for, the load would be lighter. So. most
of the supplies which are being taken
are for this purpose, sledges, food.
clothes. cooker and even emergency ra-
do and medical equipment.


Food is the heaviest item in the list,
as enough must be taken to provide
for four men for three months 1t
weighs about 800 pounds. Then comes
clothing, weighing about 300 pounds;
camping equipment, weighing a little
over 100 pounds; travelling equipment,
including sledges. weighing IS pounds;
navigation instruments. weighing 20
pounds; radio gear, weighing So pounds,
and medical equipment, weighing
pounds.


Studied Lists Carefully.


Comdr. Byrd went over these lists
time and again this Winter, consulting
various members of the expedition most
directly concerned to make sure not
only that nothing essential was over
looked but also that the amount to be
taken might be brought down to the
minimum weight. Things have been
taken out of the original containers,
and put in lighter containers reduced in
every way consistent with safety. A
forced landing on the plateau would
mean a long walk home and Byrd made
his plans to meet this extreme emer-
gcncy.


Food Is, of course. the most vitality
important part of the emergency equip
nent. Maintaining is the hardest kind
of work. and a ration on which men
can keep their strength and still Dull
Sledge-loadS must not only be Sufnc1ent
in quantity but contain necessary nutri-
tional elements.


The emergency ration for the plane
consists of pemmican of the same kind
used so successfully by Amundsen and
used by the trail parties of the Byrd
expedition: biscuit containing many
valuable food elements, powdered milk.
sugar, peanut butter, bacon, condensed
soup. rolls, raisinS, tea, cocoa, chocolate
and salt This ration will provide So
ounces per man per day.


Clothes Meet Tests.


The clothes have been selected also
10 meet all conditions on the trail and
Comdr. Byrd made up his list after
experimenting all Winter and also using
the experience of men who have been
on the trail.


Each man has a fur parka and fur
pants, sleeping bag. wooden parka,
wooden pants, light windproof pants
and parka, windproof shirt. wooden
underwear, sweater. fur hat. wooden
helmet, scarf, mukluks. ski boots, canvas
boots, caribou socks, moccaSinS. wooden
socks, windproof socks, nittS of several
kinds. face, masks, safety belt and
pulling harness: also towel, sewing kit
knife. snow glasses. crampons, compass
and a few other articles.


This clothing has been varied so that
after a day of pulling and becoming
soaked with perspiration the men may
put on dry clothing and so far as pos
sible avoid the wet which has made
polar travel so uncomfortable and even
dangerous.


The camping outfit consists of a tent.
a zegka-cooker using a primuS stove.
aluminium soup bowls enameled cups,
wooden spoons. primus stove cleaner,
needles. 10 gallons Of gasoline for the
stove, boxes of solidified alcohol tablets
to light the stove. matches, snow knife,
saw. shovel, ice ak and wire.


The travelling equipment consists of
two sledges and canvas tanks to hold
the loads, sled meter, rawhide sails for
sleds, bamboo poles to be used crossing
crevasseS, skis and ski poles, straps and
repair gear for the skis, one pair snow
shoes, three lengths of alpine rope with
knots and loops and smoke bombs for
signaling.


Radio Equipment.


The navigation equipment comprises
q Bumste2d sun compass with pelorus
for use on a Jacob staff, binoculars,
pocket aneroid barometer, two Their
mometers, dividers, ruler, protractor,
four watches on Greenwich mean time,
triangle, czegka position compass,
azimuth and line of position tables,
nautical almanac, four charts, note
book. lead pencils, sextant and oil for
artificial horizon.


The radio equipment consists of a
transmitter, another transmitter for the
radio compass, antenna, receiver, storage
battery, radio helmets and spare parts.

raIiaf train dIa from SQnQIIC AnV

they ran to the forward end of the

utes after Southern Pacific passen-

The Athletics have passed the tests

The Mackmen stood off the world
champion Yankees in the first big test,
and now, after a crucial trip through
the West that started somewhat poorly,
having come back home with their big
lead substantially intact, well prepared
for the final drive.


Connie Mack has experienced too
many disappointments in recent years
to start building air castles or additions
to Shibe Park when two months of
campaigning remain, but the veteran
leader now has every reason to feel con-
fident he will hear the roar of the world
series crowd once more, after a lapse
of Is years.


The Yankees have made a gallant
fight to stay within hailing distance of
the Athletics. But the teams general
decline, which actually set in last sea-
son in spite of a glamorous world series
performance, has not been checked.


The breaks" of base ball have been
mostly against the men of Miller Hug
gins. He failed to solve his worrisome
infield problem. Waite Hoyt and George
Pipgras the two pitching aces lost some
of their effectiveness. Finally, Babe
Ruth, after a comeback that seemed to
inspire the club, has experienced fur
Their damage.


All circumstances considered the
Yankees probably will be fortunate to
keep either the Browns or the Tigers
from forcing them out of second place
before the season closes

Special Dispatch TO The Star


NEW YORK, May 15.-For two hours
today the Stock Market was strong
and active with a number of issues
forging ahead into new high ground.
Then as money frightened the list turned
irregular, volume fell of and the trend
became uncertain.


The renewal rate for call loans was
10 per cent, which was the figure at
the close yesterday. In the early after
noon money advanced to II per cent,
and even then it was in scant supply.


At o'clock it went to Is per cent.


The best that could be said was that
there was no real weakness and that
activity decreased on the decline.


Except for Packard, motor shares
we're heavy in the afternoon, although
they had been uniformly strong in the
first half of the session. Rubbers sold
off, perhaps in sympathy with the break
IN rubber futures. The oils acted dis
appointingly all day. failing to reflect
the favorable dividend news. Utilities
came down from their best, but made
good showing


Sentiment in the Street was much
mixed. On the one hand it was admit
ted that the market had shown sur
prlsing recuperatlve power, but against
this was the continued uncertainty of
the credit situation.


The market movement in the last
hour was confused in the extreme
Fractional losses were recorded by
many stocks, perhaps more than show
ed advances, but the gains were as a
rule larger in amount than the declines
Packard maintained its leadership and
sold at new record high toward the
end. Warner Brothers Pictures was
strong and the stock OF the public util-
ity holding companies held firmly In
general, the list showed its now familiar
indifference to high money.

HICKSvItLE, Long Island, August
24.-Mrs Charles A. Lindbergh, in max
ing her first solo flight at the Aviation
Country Club here yesterday proved
that her husbands condolences in her
was not misplaced by making three per-
feet take-offs and landings.


Mrs. Lindbergh had received a little
more than 10 hours of dual instruction,
Including an hour that she spent in the
air with Col. Lindbergh yesterday morn
ing, before he sent her up alone. This
does not include the time that she has
spent riding with her husband as a
passenger, but only the hours of in
struction at the country club. Ten
hours is the average time spent by fly
ing students in dual instruction, but
many take longer.


Fly Early in Day.


Col and Mrs. Lindbergh were out on
the field at $3.50 o'clock. They have
been stopping at the club while the les
sons have been in progress and have
done most Of their flying in the
morning.


The Clubs Curtiss Fledgling training
plane was ready when they stepped onto
the field. Both strapped on parachutes
and stepped into the little plane in
which Mrs. Lindbergh has received all
of her lessons, Then Col. Lindbergh
informed his wife that he was going to
ask her to fly alone.


But first they flew together for about
an hour, landing frequently and taking
off again. Mrs. Lindbergh was at the
controls most of the time, with her
instructor coaching her when it seemed
necessary.


Then the plane came down for
landing and Col. Lindbergh clambered
out He stood beside the cockpit for
a few minutes to give final instructions
and then waved her away. Mrs. Lind
bergh took off easily, circled the field
and landed. Again her instructor spoke
to her and again he sent her aloft
When she landed the second time Col
Lindbergh sent her away for still an
other fight by herself.


Landings Exceptionally Good.


Satisfied with the progress that she
was making, Col. Lindbergh went into
the clubhouse to make telephone call
while Mrs. Lindbergh was flying in the
vicinity of Hicksville. He was back on
the field when she landed the third
time.


Then he resumed his seat in the
pltne and they went up together. After
antther half hour of practice take-offs
and landings the lesson was concluded
and they returned to the clubhouse:
Members Of the club who watched
the flight said that Mrs. Lindbergh
showed no nervousness when she start
ed for her first solo. She handled the
ship easily, they said, and her take
offs and landings were exceptionally
good for first solo attempt.
Mrs. Lindbergh has flown with her
husband frequently since their mar
rage, and they always slipped away
for airplane rides when he visited her
as Miss Anne Morrow in Mexico City.
During one of their flights there they
were forced to land on a damaged un-
dercarriage The plane turned over
and Col Lindbergh carried his arm in
sling for weeks afterward.

BY the Associated Press.


ELKTON, Md, March 30.-Suspicion
that robbers had shot Mrs. Anna Ma
honey, 81, and her 53-year-old son, Ed
ward Mahoney, to death before their
farmhouse home, seven miles from here,
was destroyed by fire last night, kept
Cecil County authorities busy tonight
seeking the facts.


So complete was the destruction of
the house that but one body could be
located In the ruins. That was thought
to have been the bones of the son, but
Coroner Howard w. Green, in charge
Of the investigation, despaired of learn
ing anything about the cause Of his
death because of the condition to which
intense heat had REDUCED the bones.


Declaration Of Guy Lewis, farmer
living near the Mahoney home, and
other neighbors, that they heard shots
about IL o'clock last night nearly three
hours before the fire was discovered,
gave rise to the suspicion that some
body seeking money the Mahoneys were
thought to have kept about the house,
had shot them and then fired the
building to hide the crime.


When the fire first was discovered by
Robert williams, colored, who was pass
ing the house, it was not known GER
tainly whether the occupants had
escaped. The Elkton fire department
made a seven-rnile run, but arrived
after the fire had gained such head
way the large building could not be
saved. AS the ruins fell, Chief Nor
wood Atkinson caught glimpses OF the
bodies, and started the investigation
which led him to adopt the murder
theory.


After Coroner Green took up the In
vestigation his suspicion was turned to
Elmer Johnson, resident Of a farm about
a mile from the Mahoney home. He
ordered Sheriff Clinton G. Logan to take
johnson into custody and hold him for
further questioning, after reports were
circulated that johnson had been seen
leaving the vicinity Of the Mahoney
farm shortly before the fire was dis
covered.

Small Margaret Cockrell never cried.


Yesterday she had real need of COM
posture, and today she must feel that
crying would be futile.


When the explosion sent four of
Margaret's party to fatal injury amid
the debris of McCrory's store front,
Margaret was to bewildered to cry out.


Later at the hospital she steadily re-
fused to lose her head and as steadily
helped the nurses identify the dying.


Perhaps the horror of it all dawned
slowly. but Margaret came through
with dry eyes.


Stified Sob Escapes.


Only when someone mentioned the
shopping tour the little family party
was on, with its visions of Santa Claus
and gay Christmas decorations In the
store windows, did a stifed sob
escape her.


For the rest of the time, the 1o-year-
old girl has lain on her cot at Emer-
gency Hospital, staring at the fiat white
ceiling above her. hard.


The catastrophe fell swiftly. One
moment Margaret, her mother, Mrs.
Anna Cockrell of 4505 Arkansas avenue,
her baby sister, and two other women
were standing on the sidewalk, looking
at the decorations in the shop window.
The next and they had been precipi-
tated into q deadly pit full Of flying
concrete and debris.


Once in the big hospital. where the
dying and injured were being admins
tered to in utmost haste, the nurses
came to Margaret and asked her to
identify two women at deaths door.


And Margaret, lying on her cot,
bruised and suffering, with her finger
nails gripping the cover until they
showed white, answered their questions
staedily.


Before Margarets mother died in the
emergency receiving room downstairs
the girl identified her from garments
brought to her bedside.


Margaret spelled out the name and
address, once for her mother, and then
again when Mrs. Cockrell's aunt, Miss
Kitty Cullinan, 4505 Arkansas avenue,
was dying.


Helps Identify Third.


The child also helped identify third
member of the party, Miss Elizabeth
Dawson, a former Schoolmate and init
mate friend of Mrs. Cockrell Miss
Dawon had Joined the party downtown
to accompany them on the shopping
tour.


Although the group was bent on some
small purchases, their main purpose in
visiting the stores was to show the chill
dren the Christmas decorations, and
possibly Santa Claus.


Margaret's two-year- sister, Mary
Anne, was the fourth member of the
party to die.


The child has borne up bravely. al
though the attendants were unable to
Keep the full extent of the tragedy
from her. She escaped with minor
bruises in the accident, but will prob
ably remain at the hospital for sew
eral days to recover from the shock,

BAY OF WHALES, Antarctica, jan

disconcerting contact with killer
whales Sunday night. We had been
wondering whether they would attack
an open boat, for they are the most
vicious and sinister of living animals
and kill without difficulty-these whales
twenty-five feet long. We know now
that they will at least head for an open
boat and drive all hands onto the ice.


The short but exciting guessing con-
test with the whales came during a long
excursion made by Comdr. Byrd in a
small boat to a lead along the eastern
side of the bay. He was looking for a
possible landing place for the Eleanor
Boiling, which is due in a few days,
and which will offer an unloading prob
lem which will be more difficult than
the one now practically concluded.


He took one of the quarter boats
which was driven by an outboard motor
such as he used before successfully in
the Arctic. When he left the City of
New York and headed eastward toward
the lead, he was accompanied by
Sverre Strom, the first mate and ice
pilot; Paul Siple, the Boy Scout, and
John Sutton, who were running the
motor, and myself.

July 16, 1881.-The Union Army,
under Gen. Mcdowell. approximately
$4,000 strong, began its long-expected
forward movement from Washington
and vicinity southwark into Virginia
this afternoon. The numerous COM
panies of Regulars near Arlington
House. comprising Infantry, Cavalry and
Artillery. struck their tents and formed
into column soon after IL o'clock.


They did not surpass in promptness
Of movement and military enthusiasm
the New York 9Th, which also rapidly
formed and marched. leaving its tents
on the ground in the charge of a
guard. The 14th New York (Brooklyn)
Regiment was also part of the column
which formed on the road at the foot
Of Arlington Heights, with the Regulars
In front.


The scene from the Virginia hills in
the neighborhood Of the Toll Gate was
very inspiring. Looking toward Wash
ington, one could see regiment after
regiment coming across the Long
Bridge, their arms cleaning In the sun.
On the left the column from Arlington
was approaching with its rear lost in
the distance.


The two columns, coming from both
directions, joined at the Toll Gate and
each took its place in the line and con-
tinued marching southwark. Cheer
after cheer was heard as the regiments
greeted one another. This, with the
martial music and the sharp commands
of the officers. made a combination of
sound that was very gratifying to all
loyal Union men and women.


It was about 5 o'clock this afternoon
that the De Kalb Regiment, the last
from the Washington side of the
Potomac River. crossed the Long Bridge
and was greeted with loud cheers by
the men of the 2lst New York Regi-
ment, stationed at Fort Runyon. The
De Kalb Regiment, with the company
of Turcos in front, presented splendid
appearance, every man looking as If he
had been made to be a soldier. The
regiment was accompanied by vivan-
dieres, and was followed by long
wagon train, with camp equipment,
baggage, etc.


The whole Army was in high spirits.
The men showed their enthusiasm by
the elasticity of their step, their jokes
and their boyish abandon. Only one
class of men was low-spirited. These
were the troops left behind to guard
the Notifications close TO Washington.
They were loud in their murmurs be-
cause they were not permitted to join
in the advance movement.


There were rumors here tonight that
the Confederate general, Beauregard,
has abandoned Fairfax Court House.

BY WILLIAM X. HUTCHINSON


The Lame duck" session of the
seventieth Congress rolled along
toward its scheduled death two
weeks from today with both House
and Senate calendars crowded,
while Administration leaders sought
to complete their legislative pro-
gram.


The Jones bill. increasing penal
ties for prohibition violators, occu-
pied the Senate, while the House
debated a bill providing 44-hour
week for postal employees. Hun
dreds of other measures crowded
the calendars in both branches, and
there were indications the dying
Congress is rapidly running into
the usual closing legislative jam.


Supply Bills Worry


The Coolidge spokesmen in the
House were concerned chiefly with
getting the final appropriation bills
enacted. The naval BILL with its
funds for launching the new cruiser
building program, the legislative ap-
preparation bill financing the actlVi-
ties of Congress itself, and the Sec
ond deficiency appropriation bill,
providing funds for nearly all Gov
ernment departments, must be en-
acted before the adjournment. Once
these bills have been passed, Ad-
ministrat ton leaders will be ready
to stage obsequies for the dying
Congress.


The Senate had the Jones bill,
the Edge resolution for a survey of
the proposed Nicaraguan canal. and
the Glass bill, purchasing market
site in the District of Columbia. on
its preferential program. Groups OF
Senators, however, we're urging
action on the Dill resolution. extend
ing the life of the Federal Radio
Commission for another year; the
Fess railroad consolidation bill and
the House reappcrtionment bill.


ReappOrtiOnment Doomed


The reapportionment and the Fess
bills apparently will be killed in the
legislative jam. The radio resolution
probably will be enacted at a special
session Administration leaders ex-
pect to stage tomorrow night. There
will be other night sessions, too, be-
fore adjournment, for action. on
minor legislation affecting indi-
Viduals or local communities.


The Senate also faced another stiff
task-that of confirming number of
presidential appointments. The re-
nomination of former Gov. Pat Neff,
of Texas. to the Federal Mediation
Board, has met with opposition and
day probably will he set aside later
in. the week to settle the contro-
versy. His confirmation, while pre-
dicted by the Coolidge Administra-
ton, was by no means assured.

KANSAS CITY, January 25.-Fierce
blasts from Arctic wastes dashed Rocky
Mountain, Middle Western and South
western States alike today with the
sub-zero readings of the mountains and
upper plains being reflected in freezing
temperature along the Gulf of Mexico.


The severe weather, the coolest of the
Winter In several sections, was accom-
panied by snow, sleet and heavy rains
which doubly handicapped transporta
ton and communications. Partial relief
was in prospect by Saturday.


The upper Rocky Mountain region
experienced the lowest temperatures, but
even New Mexico, Oklahoma and West
crn Texas Shivered in near-zero weather


San Luis Valley Below Zero.


The mercury was expected to reach
30 degrees below zero in the San Luis
Valley OF Colorado today, which was one
of the coolest spots in the mountain
region. Miles City, Mont, reported 80
degrees below last night


A passenger in stalled bus on a
banked highway near Evanston,
Wyo.,' was reported to have died today.


A new record for the Winter was
established here today when the mer-
curry dropped TO degrees below zero.
Generally cold weather, with only brief
respites, has held this section since New
Year day.


Flood conditions were expected in
Southern Missouri where four inches of
icy rain fell yesterday to be followed last
night with snow and Sleet. Some high
ways already have been flooded in
Southeastern Missouri, while traffic was
paralyzed in the OZarks of Western
Missouri by zero weather which followed
rain and snow.


Snow in Northern Texas.


Snow fell in Northern Texas today
while heavy rains in the region below
the Panhandle continued. Relief from
the cold wave that was expected to
bring freezing weather to the Gulf
Coast was expected Saturday.


The drama of three groups of Yellow
stone Park employees fighting the wealth.
er to save mans life was presented in
Montana as the employees yesterday
began efforts to buck deeply drifted
snow and Sub-zero weather to reach
Jack Worth, 81, Winter keeper at Old
Faithful Inn, where medical supplies.
have been exhausted. Doctors in
Livingston and Mammoth have been
telephoning treatment instructions to
the inn for Worth, stricken with heart
disease.

feared tonight when the COMMUNISTS
will hold a mass meeting to protest
against the methods employed by the
police yesterday.


Although the. preliminary. police
report put the dead only at seven,
hospitals, where wounded men were
under treatment, announced 10
deaths. Two more victims were in
serious condition and are expected
to die.


A group of Communists, singing
the international" broke up this
afternoons session of the Reichstag.
They invaded the chamber, throwing
documents at the Socialist members.


According to the police. 20 civ
ilians and "a policemen were
wounded and upwards of 500 persons

Following the widest day Berlin

munists continued their activities

They plunged the workers
quarters into darkness by destroy
ing street lamps and electric signs

barricades using rifles and pistols
but Communist snipers from roof
top positions made their attack in
effectual. Armored cars were
finally brought up. The barrieades
were taken and the fighting be-
came less widespread after 2 a. m.
today.

Mrs. John Baker was sued by Henry
Clayton, who alleged that he was
struck and seriously injured while she
was driving an automobile. In the
same suit, Clayton sued Mrs. Bakers
husband, claiming that her husband,
he was liable for the wrongs committed
by her.


Mrs. Bakers husband demurred to
Clayton's suit. He asserted that the
automobile was owned by his wife and
had been registered in her name. He
pointed out that before the State had
adopted the married woman's act he
would have admitted his liability IN
conformity with the former rule Of law
that husband was liable in damages
for the wrongs of his wife. He con-
tended, however, that the married wom-
ans act, which enlarged the property
rights of married women, had changed
the former rule.


The court agreed with Mrs. Bakers
husband and dismissed the suit as
against him, explaining:


"At the common law husband was
liable for the wrongs Of his wife. The
reason, for the rule was the legal unity
incident to the marriage relationship.
In most Jurisdictions, statutes have
been passed which expressly or Inn
pliedly abrogate or limit the common
law liability A wife, therefore, is now
alone responsible for the tortS she
commits Of her own accord"

bridge, 75-foot span across Spring
sCreek. The third car. IN which
virtually AL the passengers are be
lieved to have been trapped and
drowned, went into the water. The
next three cars were piled upon the
bank of the creek. one of them be.
Ing partially under water.


Great Confusion Follows


Great confusion followed the
wreck, which occurred just before
sunrise in sparcely settled sec

Surgeons, nurses and train wreck.

NEW YORK, July 27-Most Of the
railroad reports for June and for the
six months to June 80 have now been
published. A review of them today
reveals the fact that in nearly every
section and In all but a few industrial
districts Of the country, trafic is at
high tide and the earlier effects Of loss
Of passenger earnings are diminishing.


In the East all of the important trunk
lines exhibited splendid gains both for
June and the half year. The Pennsyl-
vania Railroad increased its net operat-
by 30 per cent The New Haven had
nearly double net after charges, COM
pared with the same six months of
1928. New York Central earned a
greater gross in six months than for
any like period in six years.


In spite Of the reduced volume of
hard coal trafic, the Lehish Valley,
Lackawanna, Delaware q Hudson, Erie
and Reading all ended the half year
with a greater net for interest and divi-
dends than a year ago.


In the South recovery was conspicu-
GUS on such lines as the Southern Rail-
way. seaboard Air Line and Florida
East Coast. While not up to some years,
they have all come back strongly from
the depressed conditions Of 1927 and
1928.


The Northwest has produced good
trafic returns, supplemented by efficient
operations which together have pro-
iuced some record-breaking net returns.
The Great Northern stands out con-
spicuously among the roads In this ter
ritory, with q net increase over 40 per
cent

On this side of the border $40 Mexican

Shipments of fruits and vegetables
have shrunk to about one-fourth the
carlot movement at the height of the
season in October, says the United
States Market Service Review. Potatoes,
the leading item, are light even
Tor the time of year, and daily
totals are sometimes not more than
half the average requirements. Low
prices, combined with severe weather,
have tended TO restrict shipments from
distant sections, particularly from the
upper Lakes region. Combined carlot
shipments from the main crop region
are still some $4,000 cars behind last
seasons figures. Limited supplies in
city markets resulted in some price
gains early in January, usually 5 to 10
cents per 100 pounds, and sales in
western New York producing sections
made similar advance, reaching 81 to
$l.05 per 100 pounds for sacked stock
IN the Rochester district.


Prices to growers formerly 35 cents
per bushel in bulk became mostly 40
cents, but position was considered none
too strong, owing to signs of increasing
shipments from more distant sections.
Wire inquiry was reported good, and
some sales were made for Southern
markets. where prices are considerably
above general level, owing to absence
OF competing local supplies.

Gardeners and truck farmers
of Washington and vicinity
today greeted with JOY the re-
lief from the intensely dry
and hot spell which has held
the community in its grip for
more than a month.


The rain today Is the first really
appreciable precipitation which the
section has had since the first of
July. The lack of moisture, COM
bined with the blazing sun and
the extremely high temperatures
for the month OF July had caused
a serious condition to confront
farmers and gardeners unless re-
lief came when 1t did.


Through the month OF July the
precipitation, according to Weather
Bureau statistics, was 3.42 inches
less than normal. Only 1.29 inches
OF rain fell during the month. The
only real rain OF the month fell on
July /, when precipitation OF sc
inches was recorded.


Behind All Year


Since the first of the year the
precipitation has been 1.SO behind
normal.


While gardens in the city have
been almost literally burning up
and many lawns have been ruined
for the summer. farmers in nearby
Maryland and Virginia report seri.
Gus conditions.


Nearby grazing lands have been
particularly hard hit, thus working
a hardship on diary farmers who
supply milk to the Washington mar.
ket. Vegetables in the vicinity have
also suffered heavily from the
drought. Many crops. which have
not been utterly ruined, will be de-
layed considerably as the result Of
the absence of rain.


Forest Fires Reported


Danger from forest fires was also
impending when this mornings rain
broke the dry spell. Several small
fires have been reported in the par
ched territories of Fairfax County,
Va, and one fire was reported rag
ing last night near Ravensworth.
1t had been feared that this would
deveiope into serious proportions,
but the rain diminished the danger.


The rain gave Washingtonians
another ause for rejoicing today.
for, despite the inconvenience which
it caused, it succeeded In breaking
at least temporarily the hot spell
which has gripped the city. About
noon today the temperature had
risen only to the 73 degree mark,
whereas at the same time for the
last few days 1t has been hovering
around 80.

NORFOLK, Va, March 9.-The four
masted schooner Lieutenant Mengel,
with part Of her sails gone and leaking
was picked up this afternoon so miles
due east Of Cape Henlopen by the Coast
Guard cutter Manning, which is towing
her into Delaware Breakwater. The
schooner was sighted early today show
ing distress signals and requesting the
assistance of Coast Guard cutter.


The Manning was dispatched from
Norfolk to aid the vessel and found her
about O'Clock this afternoon. The
schooner had taken in considerable
water, but her crew had kept her in
fairly good condition by using the
pumps.


The vessel was bound for Norfolk from
Laval de Cora, Venezuela, and has been
at sea for almost two months. She was
last spoken on January 26 when pass
ing ship sighted her in latitude 1900
north and longitude 69.45 west The
Manning will reach the Delaware
Breakwater early tomorrow morning
with her helpless charge.

By the Associated Press.


ANNAPOLIS, Md, August 26.-After
two weeks of futile trials, Lieut.. Will
liams has given up his attempts to get
the Mercury racer, the tiny Seaplane
with which he hoped the United States
could capture the Schneider Cup speed
trophy, of the water and into the air
Department that his ship was worthy Of
competing.


The Navy speed ace abandoned his
idea yesterday after three attempts had
failed, the second Of which was under
perfect conditions, and which proved
that the 24-cylinder motor did not have
enough power to get the 4,000-pound
craft of the water and into the air for
the speed trials.


The failure leaves the United States
without an entry for the Schneider Cup.
and places England as the sole nation
to compete, the italian government
having withdrawn its team yesterday
following the death Of Capt. Giuseppe
Motta, its leading pilot, and the loss of
his plane.


williams, however, according to Lieut..
Comdr. John Poppen, who has been the
pilots spokesman, will install q new
motor In the ship, and make an attempt
to then get the craft into the air in an
effort to set a new speed record for
seaplanes over the three kilometer
course.


Sundays tests were conducted in
Eastern Bay, an arm of the Chesapeake
after the Severn River at the Naval
Academy here had been abandoned.
The first test came to grief when the
propeller vibration became too great.
The second, held under conditions de-
scribed as perfect, failed, and it was
then that officials said that the motor
simply did not have the power to get
the ship into the air. The third at
tempt failed when lack of lSufficient gas
pressure stalled the motor.


Tomorrow would have been the last
day Williams could possibly have made
a successful test and had the ship in
New York in time to sail Tuesday the
latest possible date, in time to reach
Cowes, England, for the races.

CHICAGO, January 22.-Purdue's
mighty machine has been stalled at
last, and today Michigan was the UNI
disputed leader IN the dizzy Big Ten
basket ball championship whirligig with
four victories and no defeats.


Wisconsin, which has dropped its only
game in six starts to Michigan, turned
the trick last night, upsetting the Boiler
makers, 81 to rs, at Lafayette. 1t was
one of the most stunning upsets of the
campaign, and as result Michigan
loafed into first place and Wisconsin
jumped into tie for second place with
Purdue.


1t was gentleman from Indiana,
Hank Kowalczyk, Fort Wayne, who got
most of the glory of the Badger triumph.
Kowalczyk, a 6-foot-6-inch forward,
stopped Purdues scoring ace, Stretch"
Murphy, allowing his mates to trip
through the Boilermaker defense time
and again for victory. The Boiler
makers fought hard fight, and might
have come through, but they missed 10
free throws in Is attempts, while the
Badgers shared Is out of Is chances.


Tenhopen at center and Foster at
forward were on the receiving end of
most of Wisconsin's short passes. and
together they looped the basket for 19
points. Kowalczyk scored one field goal
and two free throws, while the best
Murphy could do was to duplicate 1t.
Previously Murphy had averaged better
than Is points game.


Both teams played good defensive
basket ball. The Badgers, however.
excelled, forcing Purdue to make most
OF its shots from long distances. Glen
Harmeson was the only Boilermaker to
break through repeatedly. He scored
three field goals and missed several
short losses.

Al to 81, at Bloomington in the only

GOpherS, on the bottom of the cham

seemed much improved. Tt was the last
game for Bob Correll, Indiana guard

programmed this week, the Chicago
Ohio State game at Columbus Saturday
night. Two important northampton
ship clashes will be played, however
Notre Dame invading Northwestern and

Iowa at Iowa City Saturday night.

9. when it plays Ohio State. while Pur-

makers meet Northwestern and the

manlike apes, like the orang-utan and

logical garden at Budapest, Hugary,
where q family of three orang-utans

apes by driving one or more ape fam

trees so that the apes cannot escape and

ape sang to himself kind of moaning
song of indescribable sadness, even to

evening when poor Peter Goliath sang
his little dirge, lay down to sleep and
never awoke, more the victim of grief
and bereavement, his human compan-
ions insist, than Of any definite dis
ease.

Select large firm apples. Core
and peel them about one-third of
the way down from the stem end.
Place them in a closely covered
deep dripping pan or casserole. Make
thin sirup, using one cupful of
sugar to one and one-half cupfuls
Of water for six apples and boil it
for six minutes. Pour this sirup
over the apples, cover them tightly
and place in a medium hot oven
of 400 degrees F. Basic the apples
occasionally until they are tender,
but still whole. Remove the cover
and place one teaspoonful of sugar
in the cavity of each apple, and
sprinkle sugar over the peeled sur
face. Then place the pan under
the broiler flame until the sugar
has melted and the peeled section
Is a delicate brown. Basting once
or twice makes the apples look as
though they had been coated with
clear, melted sugar.

BY the Associated Press.


The American public will have to
begin tapering off July 10 on the long
established habit of breaking old-fash-
Toned bills and start acquiring the habit
Of spending the new variety, which are
different in size but represent the same
amount of purchasing power.


The new bills, six and e-siXteenths
inches long and two and eleven-Six-
teenths inches wide, with black and
white faces and green backs, will go
into circulation on that date as far as
the popular 81 and $40 denominations
are concerned. Those for higher amounts
will be introduced later.


The larger bills with which most
folks are familiar will continue to be
used until worn out, and for time
all orders for fresh paper currency will
be filled by the Treasury with both
varieties Recognizing that this may
cause Inconvenience. Treasury officials
are hopeful that the public will be
patient until the supply Of old-type
bills is exhausted and uniformity of
currency again established.


A distinctive paper developed in the
last few years. which can withstand
more folding than the kind now in use
has been adopted for the new currency
together with striking new designs,
making it easier for the average person
to distinguish the denominations of the
bills at glance and to detect counter
feits.

DETROIT, August 5.-A Federal pro-
hibition agent who disappeared early
Saturday In speed boat believed to
have been used by rum runners was
the object of a search on both sides
of the border today The agent, Richard
J. Sundlands, formerly Of New York,
was last seen putting out into the
Detroit River in the boat with a man
and woman taken into custody when
the craft was seized


Walter S. Petty, acting collector Of
customs. said today he did not know
whether Sundlands had met with vio-
lence or had disappeared voluntarily.


Sundlands and Milton Larson, a Gus
toms border patrol inspector. had seized
the speed boat early Saturday and the
latter had gone to report the seizure,
leaving Sundlands to guard the boat
and the man and woman who were
found aboard. Larson on his return
found SundlandS, the boat, and two
prisoners missing. Fishermen said they
saw the trio put out into the river.


Later Petty received reports that
Sundlands had been slain, but a search
along the river front failed to reveal
a trace of him.


Customs records show that the speed
boat was owned by Jack Heath, and
his wife, Maxine, but neither has been
located.

CRAIG, Alaska, october 5.-The four
Russian aviators flying from Moscow to
New York were safe here today after
their monoplane, Land of the Soviets,
had been forced down by motor trouble
at Waterfall, IL miles north of here.


Flying through severe electrical
storm and fighting a terrific wind, the
airmen narrowly escaped disaster after
both motors of the monoplane stopped.


Resumption of the flight to Seattle,
the next stop in the 12,000-mile air
journey. probably will not be possible
for a week because a new motor must
be installed in the monoplane. The
motor and supplies will be shipped from
Seattle. The left engine will be replaced
and the right motor repaired.


Leave Sitka for Seattle.


The Russians left Sitka early Thurs
day for Seattle, taking of at 6:42 am.
(Pacific Coast time). During the flight
of approximately 200 miles the plane
encountered bad weather, rain blinded
the pilots and the huge plane few only
a few feet above the water.


The left motor suddenly stopped and
the plane was swung around and headed
for Waterfall Bay, on the southeastern
end of Alaska. As the haven was
reached the other motor also quit.


Moored In Heavy Wind.


Two Russians remained with the
plane, which was moored after consid-
cradle difficulty in heavy wind. Their
companions made their way yesterday
to this small settlement on Prince of
Wales Island with the first word of
their safety.


Before their arrival anxiety for the
airmen caused the Coast Guard cutters
Unalga and Cygan to put out from
Juneau and Ketchikan to search near
Southeastern Alaska.

text:
Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, April 25.-The first
guns have been fired in the threatened
cigarette price war The United Cigar
Stores have cut prices at retail on the
Pacific Coast. The cut, however, has
not yet reached the low level attained
by the chain grocery stores, against
which the move is obviously aimed.


Recently the Schultz interests swore
war to the knife and knife to the hilt
If the chain grocers did not stop cut
ting prices on popular brands of Gig
arettes. The United Cigar Stores are
closely affiliated through various lines
with the Schultz interests. Together
they form a huge and powerful retail
chain of distribution. On the other
hand, the grocery chains are equally
powerful, If not more so. The largest
If these has $1,000 retail stores. The
struggle bids fair to be long continued
and severe, for while the tobacco chains
specialize in this type of merchandise,
their rivals have other lines on which
to depend for profits. The Schultz in
terests also have other lines in their
holdings and the United Cigar Stores
are taking on additional products for
distribution.


The price war probably will not en-
danger the individual cigar store pro-
prietors extensively. The chains have
made cuts in the past which the indi-
vidual retailer could not meet, yet he
has continued to exist, although in
smaller numbers, and to prosper.

In it's search for better things
to live with modern engineering
Is now improving the old family
ice box. Research conducted dur
ing the past summer has uncov.
cred a group of facts likely to
prove beneficial both to house,
wives and refrigerator manufac-
turers. Tests show that by SIM
pie and inexpensive measures
domestic refrigeratOrs can be
protected against harmful accu-
mutations of moisture that make
the ice melt faster and cause
exterior discoloring and disfig-
urement.


Everyone who has had expert
ence with household refrigerators
knows how the outsides of the
box become beaded with moisture
on hot humid days; how varnisn
becomes stained or whitened al
result; and how the outside
layer of wood or steel may decay
or rust.


Disadvantages less obvious, but
even more important, are the sat
uration of wood and cork with
moisture which gradually pene-
trates the exterior finish of the
box and the loosening of joints
in which moisture has weakened
the glue. This saturation brings
about a greater ice-melting rate.


Some Of the suggested improve
ments will have to be made by
the manufacturers, but the pur-
chasers can insist upon them.
They include:


First-Tighter joints. tighter
backs and sponge rubber where
doors meet front panels of box,
this latter possibly installed by
the housewife, are improvements
to look for. Air leaking into the
box by such openings especially
the heavily moisture laden air of
a humid day. meets the colder
temperature and deposits mois-
ture in the walls and insulation.
This should be avoided or inn
tied as far as possible


Second-Moist air is likely to
leak into the refrigerator walls
around the drain tube. Look for
a box that has the bottom boards
tightly fitted around this tube.


Third-The box should be well
insulated. The customary B-inch
thickness of wood plus 1-inch of
cork is considered minimum in
sulation.


Fourth - Commercial varnish
finishes ordinarily used do not
protect the wool against absorp-
ton of moisture under extreme
conditions. Two coats of alumni
mum paint finished with two
coats of white enamel proved
quite satisfactory in the extreme
tests made this summer. They
also give the refrigerator neat.
clean appearance. Housewives
can make this improvement them
selves.

CHERBOURG. France, March 28.-
The Cunard Anchor liner Transylvania,
with American tourists aboard. came
into Cherbourg shortly after IL o'clock
this morning listing sharply at her port
bow and well down after running
aground near Urville-Hague.


The passengers debarked Immediately,
none the worse for their experience ex-
cept for the shock of the sudden
grounding, which threw some of them
out of their berths.,


The accident took place in the midst
of dense fog at 4:l0 am, while the
Pennsylvania was proceeding at very
low speed. Capt. Robert Erskine finding
her fast, Immediately emptied a tank
containing 500 tons of fuel oil and was
able to get off without assistance, al
though three tugs stood by.


Contrary to first reports the vessel
was not beached after getting clear and
proceeded to Cherbourg under her own
power.


The Transylvania, owned by the
. Cunard Anchor Line, was returning
from Mediterranean cruise.


The pumps were keeping abreast with
the inflow of water this afternoon and it
was expected that the vessel would be
put into dry dock late this evening.


Seventy of her passengers leave to-
night for New York aboard the Carin-
thia. One hundred and thirty left at
noon for Paris and others were planning
to leave for England tomorrow on the
Scythia.
