LONDON, January 12-Physicians
attending King George had another
royal patient to care for today-Queen
Mary.


The Queen was reported to be suf-
fering from catarrh in common with
thousands of her subjects. She did not
take her usual drive yesterday, but her
condition was understood not to be
serious.


The Kings condition remained sta
tionary, but without any indications
that anxiety had increased, and the
royal family expressed satisfaction that
there had been no retrogression.
The week now ending is the eighth
of the Kings illness and the main trou-
bic has been the continuance of weak
ness, which is taxing all the skill of the
doctors and nurses.
The cold weather which is prevalent
with bitter and penetrating winds added
to the handicap. although all the re-
sources of science were employed to
counterfeit these unfavorable conditions.

Imagine a universe OF life without
light, Such a condition seems impossi-
BILE, yet, scientists say, there are more
than a hundred known species of land
animals and insects in North America
alone that live In a universe Of utter
darkness.


Many insects, reptiles, and sometimes
even mammals, like the ground squir-
rels and the bats, employ caves as their
temporary places of abode, but the true
cave animals-the blind insects (beetles.
crickets, mites and gnats), the eye
less fish, crustacea, leeches and the in
Vulnerable myriapods that inhabit the
dark recesSes Of caverns like the Man,
moth Cave of Kentucky, spend their
| entire lives In places where it is darker
than the darkest night. These animals
never, from their own choice, come to
light, nor are they found where the
atmosphere is far from the saturation
| point. In their habitat of continuous
night they live and breed, migrating
| upward or downward as the food sup
ply and moisture conditions require.
OF all cave animals, the white cricket
and the blind fish are probably best
known, but the group of minute crea-
tureS-the myriapods (centipede-like
animals) are. scientists believe, per-
haps more highly endowed by nature
than their better known comrades.
These animals are provided with won.
derfully sensitive antennae or feelers
resembling little strings of pearls which,
1t was pointed out, serve as eyes, ears
and possibly nose for the animal. These
antennae project notably from the side
Of the head and enable the animal
to travel from place to place with
perfect ease.


The myriapods have the habit of
spinning delicate web while travelling,
so they can retrace their path per-
fectly by following the web.


These minute insect-like creatures
run quite actively and can move back
ward with as much ease as forward.

BY the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, November 49, The
bodies of two men were recovered today
from the ruins of subway construc-
tion shack at Long Island City, where
200 men stampeded last night when fire
swept the structure. Twenty-Five men
were injured.


The men, engaged in digging a tun-
mel under New Town Greek to connect
the new Eighth avenue subway line with
Brooklyn, were in locker room prepar-
ing to go to work on the midnight shift
when the fire was discovered.


The flames spread rapidly through the
lower floor Of the building, and the men
made rush for the two stairways lead
ing down from the second floor, where
the locker room was located.


The stairways were SO low, however.
that the men had to stoop to run down
them, and the first men fell and rolled
to the bottom. Others stumbled over
them, and soon the stairways were
choked. Finding that exit blocked 9TH
ers leaped from the windows, and many
suffered broken bones and sprains in
the 15-foot drop.

YOLANDE, Ala, May 23.-Nine men
were killed and two others burned
severely in an explosion 1000 feet be-
low the surface in the Connersville
mine last night.
Officials of the Yolande Coal & Coke
Co., operators of the mine, said their
inspectors reported the blast was caused
by an overcharge Of dynamite.


Rescue Crews Fight Fire.
The bodies were recovered early today
by rescue crews who worked through
out the night fighting flames that en-
veloped the workings after the explo-
sion. The twelfth member Of the night
crew climbed from the shaft uninjured
The dead, including seven white men
and two colored, are: -'
Grover Herring.


Eugene Herring, son Of Grover Her
ring.


Bill Kimbrel.


Charley Patterson.


Mitchell Turner.


Will Kelly and Harry Kelly, brothers.
Phil Crees and Allen Pearson, colored
The injured:


Mark Hulsey, Severe Burns, recovery
doubtful.


o. E. Chastaine, badly burned, but
will recover.


George Byron, a pumper, emerged
from the mine unharmed.


All Killed by Explosion.


The explosion occurred at Z O'Clock
last night, and several hundred persons
miners and their families, crowded
about the mouth of the horizontal
shaft, awaiting word from returning
rescue crews who held hope that the
men were only trapped by the flames
and could be rescued.


The mine officials said examination
of the bodies indicated all men were
killed instantly.

Yellow Bird. awaited only the word
from his companions, Amino Lotti
sponsor of the Paris hop, and Rene
lie Fevre, navigator, to prepare the big
French plane for the air. Lotti and
LIE xFevre left yesterday for New York,
where Lotti believed he could obtain
more detailed weather reports than
were available by wire. After notifying
Assolant when the conditions clear,
they will hurry back here for the
take-off.

Minnesota's newspaper suppression law

brought on grounds that the Saturday

Appeal first was taken by its publish
ers from temporary Injunction and
the Supreme Court upheld the constitu-
tionality of the law. The present ap-
peal, the second, upon which the second
decision was handed down today, was
taken when the injunction was made
permanent.


Chicago attorneys, representing the
Civil Liberties League, which became in
terested In the case, argued on behalf OF
the Saturday Press, attacking the con-

CHESAPEAKE BEACH. Md, May
16.-The county road bridge crossing
the canal at the entrance to this beach,
which is the main highway approach
for Washingtonians and others who re-
side here during the Summers. collapsed
yesterday while truck belonging to
the Annapolis Products Co. was cross
ing the structure.


The driver of the truck and his helper
was thrown into the canal. One escaped
injuries and suffered only bath In the
cold water. but the other was cut and
badly bruised. They were taken to An
napoliS


The bridge has been in disrepair for
more than year and its condition has
been criticized. The commissioners only
recently let contract for new two
way bridge. and it was while the new
bridge was being constructed that the
accident occurred. Visitors to the
beach will suffer only short delay in
getting across the canal to the beach,
which is due to open May 25, since ex-
ira efforts will be made to complete the

CAMBRIDGE, Mass November 3d.
The Harvard Crimson, undergraduate

the Engineering School have roomed

rather than of natural affinities."


The only comment from Harvard
University on the attack was the follow

THE house plan is for the students in

8 H.N.S).-A big June moon.

From the point of view of Indy
and Anne there's nothing quite so
coy az a nice, damp. sticky-and
absolutely opaque-fog.


Happily isolated today somewhere
out in the misty privacy off here,
Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and his
bride were enjoying to the utmost
temporary seclusion afforded them
by atmospheric conditions.


Indy at Helm


Fog shrouded the little power
cruiser Mouette soon after the craft.
with Lindbregh himself at the helm.
was seen to pass Point Pemaquid
here, heading presumably for a har-
Dor anchorage.


William Wincapaw. airplane pilot
for the Curtiss flying service of
New York, was the keen-eyed scout
who saw the Mouette arrive, but not
even airplanes could peek thereafter
at the HONEYMOON yacht" which
had ridden safely through a storm
of rain, thunder, lightning and high
seas.


Fog wrapped them round about
and even stilled the betraying sound
of their chugging motor. The small
army of reporters, reinforced by
an auxiliary of photographers in
10 Nd IAf
initely checkmated, at least for the
time being.


The most popular theory as to
Lindy's intended destination was
the obvious one that he was headed
for the Ambassador Dwight D.
Morrow summer home at North
Haven, IS miles from here. From
the Morrow place, however, came
word that no preparations had been
made there for visitors so far as
could be seen. The big cottage"
and the honeymoon villa" were
both shattered and unoccupied. A
lone caretaker patrolled the premises,
evincing no intention of entertaining
guests. 1t didn't look as If Colonel
and Mrs. Lindbergh we're expected.


Watch for Boat


Meanwhile. all the summer resorts
along the coastline, from Cape Por-
poise. from which point Lindy and
Anne sailed yesterday, to North
Haven, kept a late watch for the
double eagle Crowds watched
along the waterfront in Portland,
and press planes and newspaper
automobiles scurried up and down
the coast.


But Indy and Anne were wrapped
in the seclusion of the friendly fog.

noon demolished the Holy Rosary

field estate, near woodward, burned to

ming.

dows in the nearby houses.

time, having been last used for mass

storm struck it about 4:30 The church,

feet high, was nearly IS years old. 1t
served as mission for colored people,

Mary's Catholic Church at Upper Marl-
boro.

COLORADO SPRINGS.-Automob

bed of Goals for his bacon and eggs.

which the Government can only meet
with the simplest facilities.

conveniences.

embrace at least part of every inpor-

The bombing plane was the one
which few from Dayton, Ohio, Tuesday

passed above the woolworth tower,

head, rudy duck, cinnamon teal,
avocet, silt and other short birds. It
also is favorite wintering ground for
the cackling goose, bird that breeds
on the northwest coast Of Alaska.


1t is further stated that because of
the encroachment of industrial and
agricultural development the wild fowl
have in many areas throughout the
United States lost their former homes
and stopping places, and that the Gov
eminent in its obligations under the
migratory bird treaty with Great Britain
is steadily working for the re-estab-
liShment of suitable water areas so that
the wild fowl may regain something
of what they have lost. The setting
aside of such areas strategically located
along the principal lines of migrations
will probably do more for the future
welfare of the wild fowl than any other
one measure.

selves with pie and lollipops and costly

pie. We know while eating we are
chumps, our recklessness will make us

call for oysters steWed and fried, for

works all out of gear, we swear by

street level. on the Manhattan side, be-
fore the tubes dip under the river.

ward both the front and rear of the
train as passengers nearest the fire
scrambled for safety: several riding in
the vestibule of the third car were
burned.


! Historical passengers began breaking

through the windows started the Stam-
pede for the doors. Frightened pas
eengers, coughing and choking, battled
to reach safety.

eybe by an emergency exit and assisted

cars unconscious from inhaling the
fumes and were carried from the tube.

City of Mexico Central American
lands, Colombia, Peru Ecuador. Venezu-

dream.

EANKOW, October 24-Continuous
but indecisive fighting between the Ma
tionalist forces and the religious Kuo-
minchun or peoples army was In
progress today throughout that portion
of Honan Province west of the Kinhan
Railway.


The opposing armies appeared to be
facing each other along - north and
south front, so miles west Of the rail-
way, whereas two days ago they formed
an eaSt-to-WeSt line. The present bat
tie line extends north from the border
of Hupeh Province to the Lunghai Rail
way near Chengchow.


Still 100 Miles From Hankow.


At their nearest point the Kuomin-
chun forces still were more than 100
miles from Hankow, their apparent OBJ
jective. The shifting of the battle line
resulted when the right wing Of the
Nationalist forces advanced northward
along the Kinhan Railway, driving the
rebels from the railroad zone, while the
left wing of the central governments
forces withdrew toward the southeast,
permitting the peoples army" to reach
the Hupeh border.


The Kuominchun army now is adj
vancing eastward In three columns,
hoping to regain railway territory.
Kuominchun spearheadS were aimed at
Shengchow in Northern Homan and
Yencheng, in the central part of the
province. Both cities are on the Kinhan
Railway, Yencheng BENZ about 200
miles north Of here.


Rail Capture Is Held False.


Reports that the Kuominchun forces
had captured Chengchow, junction point
of the Lunghai and Kinhan Railways,
apparently were erroneous. The rebel
army did launch a vigorous attack
against the junction city yesterday, but
the Nationalist used ormored trains,
artillery and airplanes with deadly eff
feet, repulsing the attackers.


Bodyguards of Chang Kai Shek, head
Of the Nationalist forces, arrived here
from Marking, seemingly indicating
that the generalissimo, who also is the
head of the Nationalist Civil Guard,
would arrive here soon to take command
of the central military forces.

fished out of the water and the pair

tiles for deportation.

days while the vessel made a 1,500-mile
cruise, by way of the West Indies, to
Yonkers. They had only few crackers
to eat during the voyage.

court She said something snapped"
inside when the other woman laughed,
and that she did not know what she
was doing.

defendants against charges of statu-
tory offense, preferred by Mrs. Brown.

by the numerous postponements partly
was responsible for her overweight
condition.

being cared for by relatives.

BY the Associated Press


MEXICO CITY, June Actual
negotiations for settlement of Mexico's
church-state problem are expected to
begin here Monday morning between
Mgr. Leopoldo Ruiz Flores, archbishop
of Michoacan; Bishop Pascual Diaz Of
Tabasco, and government officials.


Authoritative sources have revealed
that the two prelates, the former of
whom is understood to have received
a special papal commission for the task,
are expected to arrive here tomorrow.


United States Ambassador Dwight w.
Morrow and Manuel Teller Mexican
Ambassador at Washington, will also be
here fact labeled officially as a COIN
cidence, but which many believe to
have direct connection with the ne
gotiations. Mr.. Morrow particularly
has been foremost In his desire that
the problem which has so long agitated
Mexico be solved.


Exact nature of the negotiations be-
tween the government and the Roman
Catholic Church has not been divulged
but it is known that church officials
wasted no time in instituting them
after the recent statement OF President
Portes Gil indicating willingness to con-
slider a settlement. Some even said the
understanding had been reached and
that the proceeding this next week
would be largely in the nature OF mere
ratification.


Trouble Dates Far Back.


Although the Mexican religious prob
lem has been acute for only three years,
it really goes back much further than
that. The Mexican constitution of 1857.
fathered by Benito JuareZ contained
provisions for naturalization Of church
property and intimidation Of ecclesias-
teal privilege.


The JuareZ government was never
strong enough to enact and enforce leg
islation making the provisions effective,
and with the accession of Portirio Diaz
rs Mexican president shortly afterward
the church regained its old influence,
this continuing until the overthrow OF
Diaz in 1910 by Francisco I. Madero.


The Mexican constitution Of 1917,
given birth during the administration
OF Venustiana CarranZa, contained the
old provisions made even more rigor-
Gus. During the reconstruction admin
istration of Gen. Alvara Obregon 1920
24O, however they were allowed to pass
unnoticed. and it was not until 1926.
in the administration of President
Gales, that enforcement was attempted.


There might have been a settlement
even then save for one provision, that
requiring the clergy to register with
the Mexican government. This the
ecclesiaSticS protested. Finding the
government implacable, the espiscopate
their churches. the order taking effect
August 81, 1926.


Religious Services Secret.


Since then, nearly three years, the
only religious services IN Mexico have
been secret. Those church buildings
and cathedrals which have remained
open bore placards stating they are the
property of the Mexican government.
Priests and their superiors charged
with violations of the religious laws have
been prosecuted relentlessly many seek
ing exile, others being depcrted.


A Roman Catholic nun. Mother Con-
repcion Aceveda de la Llata, was con-
victed as intellectual author" OF the
assassination of President-elect Obre-
gon last Summer and sentenced to 90
years Imprisonment. She is now at
the Mexican island prison colony on
Islas Tres Marias. off the Western
Mexican coast. The Mexican govern
ment has accused various insurgent
movements at times with having Roman
Catholic backing, although these
charges have always been vigorously
denied by the prelates themselves.

GORDON Nebr, March 15.-The
snow-swept sand hills hold the fate of
little Melvin Reeves


The 60-hour search for the boy last
seen pursuing a hoop into a canyon on
his fathers ranch. was ended last night.
Mr.. and Mrs William Reeves, the cild's
parents, we're near collapse as they
called off the search. When the snow
melts another posse will seek the boys
body.


The army of Searchers, including 200
Indians from the Pine Ridge Reserva-
ton and Kyle. S. OAK. found themselves
snowbound early today, unable to push
through the snow drifts. which in many
places were eight feet deep.


Indians Aid in Search.


The Indians joined the hunt yester-
day, coming in wagons, trucks and on
horseback. Familiar with this country
as no white man is. they were unable
to make any progress through the huge
drifts north of the Reeves ranch. A
few of them plowed their way through
Tor about five miles, but were forced to
return.


Melvin, 6 years old, and his brother
Dwight, years Older, went to the pas
ture Tuesday morning hunting a lost
mitten. The last Dwight saw of his
brother was when the smaller boy
chased his hoop down a canyon.


Dwight reached home and his father
soon grew alarmed over Melvin's con-
tinued absence. 1t had begun misting
and the mist was turning to snow as the
father telephoned neighbors to help him
see. the child.


Faces Binding Snowstorm.


Before the searching party could ar
rive binding snowstorm ragged. BY
nightfall posse of 500 men were look
ing for the boy


The search continued through the
next day and all the following night.
Drifting snow had blocked all highways
and little progress was made.


Searchers yesterday were marooned at
the Reeves ranch and caterpillar road
tractor was sent to the ranch with food
and supplies. The tractor was to be
used to tow automobile loads of posse
men back to Gordon today.

NEW YORK, December 21.-Harbor

rammed and disabled by car float

The ferry boat was crossing from the
foot of West Forty-second street, Man.
haitian, to Weehawken, N. j., directly
across the Hudson River. Unlike the
heavy fog which prevailed when the
liner Fort Victoria was rammed by the
Algonquin in the lower bay last We'd
nesday, the weather was clear and visi-
bility good The ferry boat was bril-
liantly lighted.


In midstream the car float, which was
being toWed by a tug lashed alongside
of 1t, drove its prov into the port side
of the ferry, tearing a hole, through
which water poured into the engine
room.


The passengers, startled by the i'm
pact, rushed from the cabins as the
ferry boats siren began to scream dis
tress signals.


Amid bedlam Of answering signals,
tugs and other ferry boats converged
upon the crippled craft. The towing
tug held the prov of the car float in
the cash in the side of the West Point,
reducing the flow of water and prevent
ing the ferry boat from listing.


AS rapidly as they could be maneu-
Vred into position rescue craft were
lashed alongside and passengers assisted
off the West Point. The large electric
ferry boat Grenville Kane took $50 over

crew helped men and women through
boat to safety.

under the glare of searchlights trained

WESTMINSTER, Md, Dec. 4.
After celebrating for Is minutes,
jury in the circuit court here
last night acquitted Mrs, Viola
M. Spurrier of the death Of her
husband who was alleged to have
been murdered July 81.


Every seat in the court room,
When the verdict was rendered,
was filled with people who we're
anxious to get glimpse Of the de-
fendant. Immediately after the
verdict was given Mrs. Spurrier
slumped in her chair and became
hysterical, even though through
the entire trial she had remained
calm.


Friends Applaud


Applause by spectators greeted
the verdict, and Judge Francis
Neal Pike, presiding in the case,
rebuked them. Mrs. Spurrier was
congratulated by her friends on
establishing her innocence.


Mrs. Spurrier is 80 and the
mother of three children. She
testified her husband, twelve years
her senior, had abused her for
years. Before she was called to
the stand. the morning had been
spent examining 100 taleSmen
for jury service.


The state opened its case with
testimony intended to show that
after a quarrel in front of their
home Mrs. Spurrier, standing
three or four feet from her hus-
band fired two shots from a
pistol which she had bought and
kept hidden in the house for
several months, and that after
the shooting she told a state
policeman she should have done
it long before.


Then Mrs. Spurrier related her
story Of thirteen years of married
life, which. she said, were marked
by privation, abuse and threats
against her life. She told of the
shooting in front of the Spurrier
home, near Finksburg, on the
night of July 81.


Tells Of Threats


The pistol was bought and
carried by her, Mrs. Spurrier said,
because her husband had threat
ened many times in recent years
to kill her. On the night Of the
shooting, she continued, her hus-
band went out to get some whis-
key after saying he was going,
to put her light out"


After he returned, Mrs. Spur
rier testified. he attacked her,
ripped her dress from her Shout
der and tried to take the pistol
from her. Foley Naylor, visitor
at the Spurrier home, separated
them, and she fell to her knees.
Her husband started for her
again as she knelt, she related,
and then she fired.


Six NeighbOrs Testify


Her testimony was followed by
that of six neighbors, including
Clarence Forrest, stepfather OF
Spurrier, who said Mrs. Spurrier
was abused by her husband, and
told of threats against her life.


Naylor the only eyewitness, told
of the quarrel, but said Mrs. Spur
rier was standing and her huS-
band was crouching and advan-
cling toward her when the shoot
ing occurred.

PARIS. July 25.-France and Great
Britain today celebrated jointly the
twentieth anniversary of the epoch
making flight of the English Channel
by Louis Bleriot, the pioneer of Channel
flying, whose exploit two decades ago,
stirred the imagination of the world
and carried its author undying glory.


When Lindbergh was still a small boy
Bleriot, after startling the world by his
successful flight across the Channel, pre-
dicted, in a conversation with the late
Andrew Carnegie that within a decade
the Atlantic would be traversed just as
successfully by airplane as the 30-mile-
wide English channel. How good
prophet Bleriot was has been proved by
the brilliant performance of Sir John
Alcock and Sir j. Brown, who just 10
years ago made their flight across the
Atlantic


Both the French and British govern
ments We'd with each other in confer
ring honors upon the man who. while
aviation was in its infancy some 30
years ago. astonished the world by
bringing France and England closer to-
gether through the air.

nesday afternoon was not resumed

harbor. but the 10 passengers and rs

tagu were Mrs. Jacquellyn Duggan
Mason, womans page editor OF the

Joseph j. Mason. who were spending
their honeymoon here.


The storm was similar in character
to that which struck here in 1926. sink
ing small craft in the harbor, driving
larger vessels ashore, wrecking buildings
and leaving the city without power for
three days. At that time aerials on the
steel radio tower atop barren rocky
hill near the city were leveled and 1t
was several days before communications
with the outside was established.

day morning. Sweeping from the west
northwest the blow continued until 9
O'Clock that night, when there was q
lull of three hours. Following the lull
which denoted the passage of the storm
center, the wind came bowling in great
err fury from the southeast and con-
tjnued until Thursday night. Squalls
were occurring last night.

recovery.

county searchers and although two per-

By the Associated Press.


MEXICO CITY, May 2.-The Mexi-
can public learned today for the first
time of the final collapse of the revo-
lutionary movement in Sonora and the
imminent complete pacification of
Northern Mexico.


Newspapers were suspended and no
official bulletins issued yesterday, May
day, but bulletins posted at Chapulte-
pee today told of surrenders of rebel
forces in the north, occupation of
Nogales and Aqua Prieta and flight into
the United States of the principal rebel
leaders.


The bulletins also carried announce
ment of battle at Azogues, on the
Sonora border, which lasted throughout
Monday, April 20, and was probably the
last encounter of note of the revolu-
ton. Gen. Almazan's vanguard, deploy-
ing ahead of the main army, after pass
ing through Pulpito Canyon, ran into a
rebel ambush, arranged by the insur-
gent Gems. Caraveo, Yucupicio and ia
cinto Previno.


The ambush was not as complete as
had been planned, however, and the
federals were able to battle the rebels
throughout the day until Gen. Almazan
arrived at nightfall with reinforce
ments. 1t was too late for him to at
tack the rebels, who had intrenched
themselves, and when dawn came he
discovered they had withdrawn during
the night. His report said that Cara
veo and Yucupicio had fled to the
mountains. Trevino was believed here
to have escaped into the United States


The government bulletin said that
Gen. Jose Gonzalo Escobar, defeated
rebel generalissimo. had taken tempo
rary refuge in the mountains and
would try to reach the United States
through some isolated port of entry.

J. H. Tilden, pilot of the Berliner
Aircraft Corporation of Alexandria, Va,
narrowly escaped fatal injuries yester-
day when he leaped in his parachute
from a disabled plane less than 200
rect from the ground. He fell a few
moments before the plane crashed to
earth scarcely 10 feet away. The plane
iell across the partly opened parachute.
The accident occurred on the Rich
burn farm. three miles south Of Alex
andria.


Although he landed heavily, Tilden
was unhurt and walked to the Hyba
Flying Field to obtain assistance. When
word of the accident was received at
Boiling Field aviators from both the
Army and Navy posts set out to look for
the wreck. A pilot from the naval
station was the first to locate Tuden,
who waved back that he was unhurt.


Leonard G. Frye, the first to reach the
scene, said he was standing outside the
barn watching the machine when the
engine suddenly stopped directly over
the building, and the plane went into
a tail spin. Ae he neared the ground
the motor again started, but the pilot,
apparently realizing he could not right
the plane, jumped with his parachute.


Tilden said it was test plane being
tried out for just such emergencies.
and that his principal difficulty when
he jumped was trying to keep clear OF
the machine. The plane was completely
wrecked and the engine buried itself
two feet into the ground. .


Surrounding roads were filled with
automobiles, following the crash, which
occurred in such an obscure place that
few of those who sought its location
were successful. The exact point was
on the road about mile below Penn
daw, and about half a mile on hill
side from that road. Several pilots
from Hybia Valley said they few over
the scene of the crash several times
before observing the pilot, who was
waving his coat at them.

Then she saw on the floor at her

She tore open the envelope With

LACY and his satellite are dead. You

Putting the letter in her handbag,

Audrey was so used to mysteries now

NAL, Who was this mystery man, this

She read the letter again and liked

S. S. BERENGARIA, September
3O-Although but two days out from
Southampton, Miss Ishbel Macdonald,
daughter of the prime minister, has
made herself a great favorite with
other passengers, who are delighted
with her radiant personality and quiet
charm.


Saturday, her first night out, she
danced until late with British and
American fellow passengers. She arose
early Sunday and fraternized and par
ticipated in the ships social activities
until before retiring. She dances well
and knows the modern steps.


Passengers particularly were touched
with the guard she maintained about
her fathers quarters Sunday morning
to prevent his being disturbed, realizing
he wished TO rest as much as possible
of this watch,ulnesS they both missed
Church of England services aboard ship
yesterday morning. since the premier
did not awaken until All hour before
noon.


Miss Ishbel accompanied her father
for round after round of Strolling about
the big ship during the day, sometimes
leaving him for other companions.
Sunday she wore red walking suit
with darker red coat and went most
of the day without hat.


The prime minister spent several
hours yesterday on the sheltered after
deck with his pipe and book, but
the bugle announcing dinner caught
him at his walking on the broad
promenade.


The Berengaria is due in New York
Friday. Mr.. Macdonald is on the way
to Washington to confer with President
Hoover about armament


Prime Minister Macdonald is being
favored with excellent weather ON his
peace" voyage to America.


The prime minister has been taking
advantage of the clear conditions,
arising early and taking the prolonged
deck constitutional before having break
fast in his suite.


The way in which the premier has
taken part in the ordinary life OF the
ship ever since starting has been one
of the most notable features OF the voy-
age thus far. He has been seen con-
stantly at various parts OF the big boat
and 1t Is seldom that he rests in his
cabin during the daytime.

Japanese fishermen, who supply

their annual drive against schools
of sharks, which are driven in from
the open sea by the rough weather
each winter and become so bold
that they steal fish right off the
fisherman's hooks. Two drives

limped into port here after Coast

The trio-Nels Jensen, 80, Wauke-

rough seas, and made port at South

wind from the northeast to aid them,

All branches of Government revenue,
as figures were shaped up this week
in preparation for the termination on
June 80 of the official fiscal year, dis
closed advancing totals. and gave fairly
representative evidence of active
national business conditions. Partic-
ularly. the June collections of miscel-
laneous internal revenue, which

playing cards, amusement admissions,
and the like, all items of general dis
tribution, ran up nearly to $4,000, 900,
against about S40,00o,000 for the same
month last year.


Railroad traffic volume, reported out
Of Washington for the week, was still
engaged in setting new high records.
Congressional action, by reason of an
adjournment of that body, was not
factor in affairs, and the Federal Re-
serve Board maintained its recent
status of Withholding action as to bank
rates and credit matters.


Commercial Transactions.


Commercial transactions during the
period ended June 90, as reflected by
check payments, were larger than in
either the preceding week or the cor.
responding week of 1925" said the
Commerce Department weekly review
of the business situation at home and
abroad.


Activity in steel plants, while un-
changed from the previous week,
showed a considerably higher rate of
operation than for the same week of
last year. The production of crude
petroleum and bituminous coal for the
latest reported week showed gains over
both prior periods. The distribution of
commodities, as indicated by the load
ings of freight cars covering the latest
reported week, was substantially
greater than at this time last. year.


THE general level of wholesale prices
showed a further gain over the pre- ced-
ing week and was only slightly lower
than year ago. Iron and steel prices
advanced over both prior periods, while
cotton prices were lower than for either
the previous week or the corresponding
week of 1928. Loans and discounts of
the Federal Reserve Banks were larger
than during either the previous week
or this time last year. Interest rates
on both call End time loans were easier
than during the preceding week, but
substantially greater than a year ago.
Bond prices showed no change from the
previous week. but, rejecting the higher
interest rates, were lower than last year.
Stock prices showed a considerable gain
over the previous week ana were SUD-
stantially higher than year ago. Busi-
ness failures were also fractionally
greater than during the preceding week,
but were fewer than during the cor
responding period Of 1928.


Cotton Receipts.


Receipts of cotton were greater than
for either the previous week or the cor
responding period Of last year. Receipts
of cattle and hogs at the principal pri-
mary markets during the latest reported
week also showed declines from the
previous week. Receipts of cattle were
smaller and those of hogs greater than
year ago. Wheat receipts showed a
substantial gain from both prior
periods"


In Canada, the review said that
merchandise movement through dis
tribution channels had been speeding
up. In Cuba, in spite of continued low
prices for sugar, it was estimated that
general conditions were better than in
the same month last year. South Amer
lean countries, aside from Argentina,
were represented as experiencing con-
siderable business depression.

With tiny hands f1uttering he sketched flash
ing impressions of his large and faithful wife
waiting in Bologna, like the lady in Mother
Goose-for a little husband, no bigger than
her thumb-with beautiful manners and the
utmost delicacy in kissing lady's hand.


Imagine ones husband in high chair at
breakfast! Picture the small count and his
tiny lady after a late show going sleepily into
q big hotel room, where the bed must have
looked to them like load Of hay. Continental
beds are mountains of eiderdown.


Barnum gave her a comfortable ur-poster,
built to her measure, but that was left behind
In Middleboro. So was the Cinderella coach.
The three travelled in cabs that must have
seemed like moving vans, and in trans and
buses that were mountains to climb


Years ago. in the old Barnum days, Primo
had played in the same show with Gen. Tom
Thumb and had known Lavina as a young
woman the wife of his friend. Her sister,
Mime Warren, married Commodore Mutt and
at one time they were all in the show to-
gether.


The general died and two years later his
widow and his friend were married. For half
lifetime she has been the wife Of Count
Magri yet who has ever thought Of her other
than as Mrs. Tom Thumb?


The Kingdom CT Little People passed. and
went into Winter quarters. The midgets who
were fortunate joined other groups. Little Sing
Hpoo died and never had the glittering we'd
ding they had planned for him.

There were no signs of life. Shutters
covered the windows. On the door was
n printed sign indicating that German
officers had been billeted there.


The Frenchman crossed the road and
with shaking hand pulled the bell. No
one answered. Still staring at the closed
shutters. he backed away like a man in
a trance. He backed until he reached
our car. against which he leaned, pale
and trembling.


Suddenly the door swung open and
an aged woman servant appeared
She was leading a beautiful baby girl
with wealth Of golden curls.


The officer threw out his arms and
took one quick step toward his child,
and then he halted. The tot had
jumped back behind nurses ample
skirts and was peeping out in fright.
Mother undoubtedly had told her many
times during the German occupation
that men in uniform were bad and to
be avoided. The field blue of France
meant nothing to this child who had
been all her short life under German
rule. Our passenger was stranger to
his own flesh and blood, and he was
under grave suspicion.


The half-blind eyes of the old nurse
had by this time recognized the master
and she was holding out her hands TO
him and repeating monsieur. monsieur
over and over in ecstasy. He crossed
and grasped her hands But his baby
drew back still further behind the pro-
tecting skirts.


The door at The end of the long hall
opened and comely young matron
came through to see what was going on.
When she was halfway along the
passage she caught sight of her hus-
band on the sidewalk. She stopped;
her hand few to her breast, and she
swayed for second as though she were
about to fall. Then with sobbing cry
of JOY she fairly hurled herself into his
arms.


Our motor was already moving away,
for outsiders weren't needed to COM
plete the scene. Thus we left them,
with nurse beaming on the happy cou-
pie; and Curly Head looking with
round. troubled eyes at this strange
man who had appropriated her mother
so completely without word


But couldn't help looking back, and
my last glimpse Of the picture showed
Curly Head gradually emerging from
the folds of nurses skirts-a tentative
overture of friendship.

CHICAGO, May 4-One hundred
and twenty-four politicians, public Off
Gals and hoodlums today stood formally
accused of law violations, the climax to
persistent investigations by Federal and
county grand juries.


The county grand jury yesterday in
dicted IS in connection with the Chi
cago sanitary district graft scandal, in
Guiding six trustees and the former
president, while the Federal grand jury
returned indictments against 81 persons
alleged to have been members OF the
Chicago Heights booze ring. Several
were public officials.


lice CAPTAINS. were named earlier in the
week in connection with the slot-ma-
chine graft scandal.


Payroll Padding Charged.


The sanitary district investigation
began soon after the November election,
when it was disclosed that more than
1000 persons, including several legis-
lators and other officials who admitted
they did little or no work, were on the
pay rolls. Expenditure of approximately
81 600 900 for 4-mile-long cinder
bride path and other alleged wasteful
and illegal expenditures were revealed
as the investigation progressed.


Among those indicted in the sanitary
district probe were:


Timothy j. Grove, prominent Demo-
cratic leader and former president OF
the Sanitary Board: James M. Whalen,
also a prominent Democrat, who was
reelected trustee in November Frank
J. Link, John K. Lawler and August w.
Miller, Republicans, and John j. Touhy,
Democrat, trustees held over from last
IL Y
chairman of finance committee of old
board and member of new board; Mar
tin j. O'Brien, chief clerk of district
under Grove and chairman of the man
aging committee of the Democratic
party in Cook County; Henry E. Wallace,
chief deputy clerk under Grove: Morton
Kallis, head of a printing firm said to
have received 100000 from the board
for printing 100000 copies Of Groves
annual message.


The indictments included charges of
conspiracy, embezzlement and illegal
diversions of public funds, all the
trustees and former officials being
charged with all three. Some of the
charges were based on allegations that
the district spent more than $250,000
illegally. Bonds on each indictment
were set at $4,000.


Capone Not Indicted.


The Chicago Heights liquor investi-
cation was launched more than a year
ago by Federal authorities after a reign
of terror had held sway in the suburbs
for several years, accounting for nu-
merous murders. So powerful was the
alleged liquor syndicate that public Off
Gals were cowed and respectable citi-
zenS coerced into recognizing its right"
to operate openly without interference.


"Scarface" Al Capone, gangster chief
tain, was Subpoenaed to appear before
the grand jury and came from his VIM
ter home at Miami, Fla, to testify. Fed
eral officials said that insufficient evil
dence to warrant indictment of Capone
had been obtained.


The syndicate was said to have fur
nished more than 100000 gallons of
contraband liquor, valued at $4,000 900,
to the liquor trade since January /,
1925. Stills were allowed to operate
openly, the Government charged, by the
towns officials and police after the boot
leggerS had demonstrated by shotguns
and pistols that they intended to have
their way. Subsidies later were paid, i
was charged, to officials.


Former Police Chief Indicted.


Those indicted included Bahne Car
nilsen, former chief of police and pres
ent postmaster of; Chicago Heights. and

eral prominent politicians were named

America.

quarry in the Iolo country. west of

run by bandits. The panda is distinct
but related to both bear and raccoon

time the arrivals were busy answering
questions.

severe cold of the nights spent in sleep

Comdr. Byrd, with Dean Smith as
pilot and Malcolm Hanson as radio
operator, Jew on Monday to the three

tains. He and Hanson remained with

CLEVELAND, Ohio, May 16.-An
army of volunteers, taking orders from
police officials and executing hem with
amazing coordination, performed he
roic rescue work in the Cleveland Clinic
short time after the blast left Its trail
Of dead there yesterday.


Men from all walks of life-men in
gray and blue business suits, overalls,
taxi uniforms, even rags-stood at the
back of policemen and helped in taking
the injured end dead from the building
While it still was filled with death
dealing gases.


All Vehicles Communicated.


Inspector George J. Matowitz, who
rushed from central police station with
flying squads, found huge pillows of
smoke and gas enveloping the structure,
and with other police officials he COM
Wandered all vehicles in sight as am
balances and then pressed every avail
able man in the vicinity into duty as
fast as they volunteered.


While delivery trucks drays. transfer
wagons and private automobiles stood
ready to take away the dead and in
jured, butchers. grocers, dentists, sail
orS. brokers' taxi drivers and clerks,
working in small groups under uniform
ed men. waded through water left by
the fire hose and tore away distractions
as they helped carry on the first rescue
work.


Back of the clinic the fence was lined
with volunteers, grim-faced men, wait
Ing their call. At word from a fire.
man or policeman they plunged in and
performed the duty assigned them.


Many Made Silent by Horror.


Many of these volunteers, white of
face, with the horror they met inside
the walls of the clinic tomb, could talk
but little while they rested from their
labors. cit was terrible" was about
all they could say.


One volunteer said, ct never hope
to have look at anything so horrify-
ing again. AS far as you could see
were bodies, bodies, bodies, down those
stairways. It was trrible. those twist
ed arms and legs, screaming men and
vomen-bodies and screams


Firemen, too, made heroic rescues.
Hook and Ladder Company No 8, bat
ting flames and fumes, went to the
top of the building on an 85-foot lad
Ger, which, by chance, went into sery-
ice only last week.


Under Battalion Chief Michael
Graham two men Of this company,
Howard McAllister and Peter Rogers,
chopped their way through the sky
light, put ropes under their arms and
were lowered into the building Then
they swung themselves until they
gathered enough momentum to drop
inside the mezzanine rail which circles
the fourth floor.


Bodies Packed Four Deep.


Both firemen said they found bodies
packed four deep In the space between
the stairway and the elevator. Other
firemen knocked open a trap door in
the roof, and McAllister and Rogers
lifted Is persons out into the open air.
Though several were dead, others were
saved by lung motors used there on
the roof.


Companies of firemen, some with
gas masks, some without, worked their
way through the fume-choked build
ing, many of them with volunteers as
assistants as they searched for in
jured and dead.

DUTCH HARBOR, Alaska, December
14.-Reports that seven volcanoes on
the Eastern Aleutian Islands and the
Southern Coast of the Alaska Peninsula
were Spouting flames and spreading
dense sulphur smoke in the first general
outburst in that region since 1927 was
believed by marine men here today to
indicate that island and coast contours
there are again being altered.


The crew of the steamer Starr arrived
here with reports that the volcanoes
Katmai, Pavlof, Mageik, Kagami!,
Akutan. Chiginagak and Shisaldin were
unusually active. All of the volcanoes
are remote from civilization, but few
Indian settlements are on the islands
near some of the peaks.


Akutan, of 4.100 feet altitude, spread
lava over the island of that name last
May and part of the top Of it was blown
off In the Summer and Fall of 1927
about 20 volcanoes were violent in the
region.


Shishaldin was reported here as being
the most active. This peak, rising
10000 feet on Unimak Island near the
village of Sisaguk, always one of the
most spectacular, opened new crater
in 1914.


There are at least 600 inlets which
never have been charted and frequently
are changing in this region. The
Bogoslof Volcano, which lowered 1000
feet above the sea in 1923, entirely dis
appeared under water after that, only
to burst out again in 1896. Fire Island
rose from the sea in 1888.

PEKING, February 25.-American
money for relief of starving millions in
China is beginning to arrive and is be-
ing sent by the China International
Famine Relief Committee to spots where
conditions are worst


According to the latest estimate Of
the committee between 10000 900 and
2O,OO0,OO0 people are starving in the
vast central district of China. The
worst affected areas are Chahar. beyond
the Great Wall; Shensi, Kansu and
Southwest and Western Honan.


In Shensi entire families have been
driven to suicide, the children taking
their lives first and the mother and
father last. Hundreds whose homes
have been burned have taken refuge in
caves. In the Sienyang and Chinyang
districts whole villages are facing star
walton and hundreds are dying daily in
the streets.


Tens of thousands are trying to keep
alive on such food substitutes as null
berry leaves, cotton seed with the lint
still adhering, wild grass ground to pow
der and baked cotton seed cake.


Besides the American relief seven
Chinese organizations whose scope is
country wide have been assisting. Local
governments have helped, too, in some
cases.

ever heard from them after they
passed the Irish coast.

Azores in the wreck of his plane
on July 13. His companion, Casi-
mir Kubala, survived.

DETROIT, October 12.-MrS. Lois
Dodge Manning, former wife of Horace
z. Dodge, jr., yesterday was granted
a divorce from Benjamin Franklin
Manning, her second husband and for
merly a United States Army lieutenant
stationed in Hawaii.


Katherine Berg, Mrs. Manning's per-
sonal maid, was the only witness in the
hearing today before Judge Theodore
j. Richter Conclusion of the case had
beeh delayed until the recovery of the
maid from an illness which prevented
her appearance in court several weeks
ago, when Mrs. Manning testified.


The maid said that she had never
seen Manning strike Mrs. Manning, but
that Mrs. Manning, In the presence OF
her husband, had described his assaults
and that he had expressed regret. FIRE.
ouently, the maid declared, Mrs. Man.
ning's face was marked by bruises.


Miss Berg testified that on the honey
moon trip Manning was locked up
aboard ship between San Francisco
and Hawaii because of his cruelty to his
wife.


Mrs. Manning and Manning were
married in September, 1927, and lived
together for only six weeks. She was
divorced from her first husband, Horace
